episodes.text: Began writing his autobiography at Twyford, the country seat of Bishop Shipley, during a week of leisure in 1771.
Josiah Franklin emigrated from England to Boston with his wife and three children around 1682 to practice Nonconformist religion freely.
Uncle Benjamin visited Josiah in Boston and lived with the family for several years during Franklin's boyhood.
Uncle Benjamin taught Franklin his personal shorthand system, which Franklin later forgot from disuse.
Franklin searched parish registers at Ecton, Northamptonshire and found family births, marriages, and burials recorded back to 1555.
Sent to grammar school at age eight; Josiah intended him for the Church as 'tithe of his sons'.
Withdrew from grammar school after less than a year due to expense of college education; sent instead to Mr. George Brownell's school for writing and arithmetic.
Taken home at age ten to assist Josiah in the tallow-chandler and soap-boiling business for two years.
Led playmates in secretly taking building stones to construct a wharf at the salt marsh; was discovered, corrected by his father, and learned that nothing useful can be dishonest.
Josiah Franklin died at age 89; Abiah Franklin died at age 85; Franklin placed a marble gravestone over their burial site in Boston.
Josiah considered the cutler's trade for Franklin and sent him on trial to cousin Samuel Franklin in Boston, but withdrew him when Samuel demanded a fee.
Signed indentures as an apprentice to brother James at age twelve, to serve until age twenty-one with journeyman wages in the final year.
Brother James returned from England in 1717 with a press and type to set up a printing business in Boston.
Composed and sold ballads — The Lighthouse Tragedy and a song about Blackbeard — as a teenager; first sold well but father discouraged verse-making.
Conducted a written debate with John Collins on the education of women; father critiqued his writing as lacking elegance and method.
Adopted a vegetable diet at age sixteen after reading Tryon; negotiated half the board money from James and used savings to buy more books.
Taught himself arithmetic from Cocker's book, then read navigation, Locke on Human Understanding, and du Port Royal's Art of Thinking.
Discovered the Socratic method through Xenophon and an English grammar; adopted it as his mode of argument, later moderating to modest diffidence in expression.
James Franklin began printing the New England Courant around 1720 or 1721 — the second newspaper in America.
Anonymously slipped essays under the printing-house door at night; they were praised by James's literary circle, who attributed them to men of learning.
James was imprisoned for a month by the Assembly over a political piece in the Courant; Franklin managed the paper during the imprisonment.
The Assembly ordered James Franklin to cease printing the Courant; the paper was transferred to Franklin's name with secret new indentures to retain his labor.
Exploited the secret indentures to assert his freedom from James, then found himself barred from every Boston printing-house by James's intercession.
Escaped Boston secretly at age seventeen with Collins's help — passage arranged under false pretenses — and arrived in New York with very little money.
William Bradford in New York could not employ him but directed him to his son in Philadelphia, where a hand had just died.
Crossing the bay toward Amboy, rescued a drunken Dutchman who had fallen overboard during a squall.
Arrived in Philadelphia on a Sunday morning in October, dirt-poor and exhausted, with a Dutch dollar and a shilling in copper after a grueling overland and river journey from New York.
Walked up Market Street eating a bread roll, passing the door of Mr. Read — where Deborah Read saw him and thought him ridiculous.
Fell asleep in the Quakers' meeting-house — the first house he sat in in Philadelphia.
Called on Andrew Bradford Jr. in Philadelphia; Bradford could not hire him but directed him to Keimer and offered lodging.
William Bradford Sr. accompanied Franklin to Keimer's shop and artfully drew out all of Keimer's business plans through feigned ignorance.
Survived fever after Amboy by drinking cold water plentifully; recovered overnight and continued journey to Philadelphia on foot.
Lodged at Mr. Read's house (Deborah's father's) through Keimer's arrangement; made a more respectable appearance to Miss Read than on first arrival.
Governor Keith sought Franklin out at Keimer's shop, took him to a tavern, and proposed setting him up as a printer in Philadelphia with the public business of both governments.
Returned to Boston around April 1724 after seven months away, bearing Governor Keith's flattering letter of recommendation to Josiah.
Visited James's printing-house in fine new clothes with silver in his pockets; the display offended James, who said he could never forgive the insult before his people.
Josiah flatly refused Governor Keith's plan as premature, saying Franklin was too young to be trusted with so important a business.
Josiah nevertheless approved Franklin's return to Philadelphia, advising steady industry, prudent parsimony, and avoidance of lampooning — and promising help when Franklin turned twenty-one.
Collins planned to go to Philadelphia as well and set out ahead by land to Rhode Island, leaving his book collection to travel with Franklin to New York.
Stopped at Newport, Rhode Island, and visited brother John, who received him very affectionately.
A Quaker matron on the Newport-to-New-York passage warned Franklin away from two young women passengers she judged dangerous; Franklin heeded her advice and avoided them in New York.
The two young women Franklin had been warned about were found by the captain to have stolen a silver spoon and other goods from his cabin and were punished.
Found Collins at New York, already deep in daily drunkenness and gambling since his arrival; paid Collins's lodgings and defrayed his expenses to Philadelphia.
Governor Burnet of New York invited Franklin to visit after hearing from the captain that the young passenger carried many books; they conversed at length about books and authors.
Collected Vernon's 35-pound debt on the road to Philadelphia; Collins continually borrowed from it until nearly all was gone, causing Franklin great distress.

On the Delaware, Collins refused his turn at the oar; Franklin pitched him overboard when he threatened violence; Collins eventually left for Barbados with a West India captain and was never heard from again.

Governor Keith, on learning Josiah would not set Franklin up, offered to do it himself — told Franklin to make an inventory of printing supplies (~100 pounds sterling) and to sail to England on the ship Annis to choose the types.

Becalmed off Block Island on the first voyage from Boston, broke his vegetarian resolve and ate cod, reasoning that fish eat each other — thereafter ate as others did, only occasionally returning to vegetables.
Tricked Keimer into a three-month vegetarian diet as a condition of the sect proposal; Keimer suffered greatly, eventually caved and ate a whole roast pig before the guests arrived.
Made some courtship to Miss Read before departing for England; her mother thought it prudent to wait until after his return and establishment in business.
Exchanged some promises with Miss Read before sailing for England.
Franklin, Ralph, Osborne, and Watson formed a literary circle — Sunday walks near Schuylkill, reading aloud and conferring on what they read.
At a poetry contest Franklin passed off Ralph's verse as his own; Osborne lavishly praised it; the trick was revealed at the next meeting.
Watson died in Franklin's arms a few years after the Philadelphia literary circle period — much lamented as the best of the set.
Governor Keith kept putting Franklin off when he called for the promised letters of recommendation and credit; at Newcastle the secretary said the letters would be sent on board — they never were.
Sailed for England with Ralph (who abandoned his wife and child); Colonel French gave Franklin notice on board; Mr. Denham befriended him on the voyage.
Arrived in London 24 December 1724; discovered in the Channel that Governor Keith had sent no letters — the bag contained only a letter from the knave Riddlesden, not Keith.
Denham revealed Keith's true character — no credit, no letters, only empty promises; advised Franklin to find printing work in London and return to America better equipped.
Delivered Riddlesden's letter to Andrew Hamilton on arrival, warning him of a scheme against him involving Keith; Hamilton became Franklin's friend and benefactor thereafter.
Got work immediately at Palmer's printing-house in Bartholomew Close; stayed nearly a year.
Spent earnings with Ralph on plays and amusements; consumed all fifteen pistoles and was kept constantly unable to pay his passage home.
Wrote only one letter to Deborah Read from London — to say he was unlikely to return soon — and gradually forgot his engagements to her; called this another great erratum.

At Palmer's, composed for the second edition of Wollaston's Religion of Nature and wrote a metaphysical pamphlet — 'A Dissertation on Liberty and Necessity, Pleasure and Pain' — calling it another erratum afterward.
Made acquaintance with bookseller Wilcox in Little Britain who lent him books from an immense second-hand collection.

Pamphlet led to acquaintance with surgeon Lyons, who introduced him to Dr. Mandeville (author of Fable of the Bees) and Dr. Pemberton; Pemberton promised to introduce him to Newton but it never happened.
Sir Hans Sloane visited to see Franklin's asbestos purse curiosity and paid him handsomely for it.
Ralph moved in with a milliner lodger, then left for a country school in Berkshire under the name 'Mr. Franklin'; recommended his companion Mrs. T to Franklin's care.
Attempted familiarities with Mrs. T (another erratum) — she repulsed him and told Ralph; Ralph declared the debt cancelled and friendship ended.
Left Palmer's for Watts's, a greater printing-house near Lincoln's Inn Fields, where he stayed for the rest of his London time.
At Watts's, initially worked at press to get bodily exercise; drank only water while fellow workmen guzzled beer — earned the nickname 'Water-American' by being stronger than the beer-drinkers.

Refused to pay the compositors' bien venu fee at Watts's; endured weeks of chapel-ghost mischief until compelled to comply — convinced thereafter of the folly of being on ill terms with those one lives with continually.

Proposed alterations to chapel laws at Watts's and carried them; persuaded many workmen to switch from beer to water-gruel breakfast — cheaper and clearer-headed; stood security for their beer debt on Saturday nights.
Moved lodgings from Little Britain to Duke Street, opposite the Romish Chapel — agreed terms at 1s 6d per week after landlady reduced rent in exchange for his company and protection.
Taught Wygate and a friend to swim; at Chelsea swam from near Chelsea to Blackfriars performing many feats of activity, to the admiration of the company.
Wygate proposed they travel Europe together working as printers; Denham dissuaded Franklin and advised him to return to Pennsylvania.
Denham proposed Franklin return to Philadelphia as his clerk at 50 pounds a year Pennsylvania money to manage his store and eventually be sent to the West Indies on commission.

Sir William Wyndham summoned Franklin about teaching his sons to swim before their travels; Franklin could not undertake it due to his uncertain departure — reflected that a swimming school in England could have made him money.
Sailed from Gravesend 23 July 1726; formed at sea a plan for regulating his future conduct in life.
Landed in Philadelphia 11 October 1726; found Keith no longer governor, superseded by Major Gordon.

Learned that Deborah Read, despairing of his return, had been persuaded to marry Rogers the potter — an unhappy marriage from which she soon separated; Rogers ran away to the West Indies and died there.
Worked with Denham at his Water Street store in Philadelphia; Denham counselled him like a father and they lived together very happily.

In early February 1726-7, just past his twenty-first year, fell severely ill with pleurisy and nearly died; recovered but remarked with dry humor he regretted having 'that disagreeable work to do over again.'
Denham fell ill at the same time; his illness carried him off; he left Franklin a small legacy in a nuncupative will.
After Denham's death, Holmes advised Franklin to return to printing; Keimer offered large wages to manage his printing-house — Franklin reluctantly accepted.

At Keimer's found five indentured or low-wage hands — Meredith, Potts, an Irish John, George Webb, and David Harry — all raw and needing training; soon perceived Keimer's scheme to use him to train cheap hands and then dismiss him.
At Keimer's, contrived a type mould from letter puncheons to supply missing sorts — became factotum: compositor, inkmaker, engraver, warehouseman.
Quarrelled with Keimer when Keimer rebuked him publicly from the street; walked out on the spot.
Meredith proposed a partnership: his father would furnish capital for press and types from London; Franklin's skill would be the other half of the stake.
Returned to Keimer when Keimer needed Franklin for the New Jersey paper-money job; contrived the first copperplate press seen in the country; went to Burlington for three months.
At Burlington made acquaintance with principal people of the province — Judge Allen, Bustill, Pearson, Cooper, Smiths, Decow — who became lasting friends.
Isaac Decow, surveyor-general of New Jersey, predicted Franklin would soon work Keimer out of business and make a fortune in Philadelphia.
Settled with Keimer and left him; rented a house near the market with Meredith and Godfrey the glazier.
First customer — a countryman brought by George House — paid five shillings; Franklin called it more pleasure than any crown since earned.
Samuel Mickle stopped at the door of the new printing-house to warn that Philadelphia was a sinking place and the printing venture would fail.

Formed the Junto club in the autumn preceding the printing-house opening — Friday-evening meetings with written queries and essays, rules against positiveness, and debates in the spirit of inquiry after truth.
Breintnal procured from the Quakers the job of printing forty sheets of their history — worked a sheet a day composing, Meredith at press, often finishing distribution past eleven at night.
One night a composed form broke and two pages were reduced to pi — immediately redistributed and recomposed before going to bed, demonstrating the industry that gave the new shop its reputation.
Foolishly confided to George Webb the plan to start a newspaper; Webb told Keimer, who published rival proposals and employed Webb.
Wrote the Busy Body series for Bradford's paper to counteract Keimer's newspaper proposals; Breintnal continued the series for several months.
Keimer ran his paper for three-quarters of a year with at most ninety subscribers, then offered it to Franklin for a trifle; Franklin took it and it proved extremely profitable within a few years.
Wrote spirited remarks on the dispute between Governor Burnet and the Massachusetts Assembly in the new paper; they struck principal people and brought them all as subscribers within a few weeks.
Reprinted elegantly and correctly Bradford's coarse, blundering print of the House's address to the governor; the Assembly voted Franklin and Meredith their printers for the ensuing year.
Mr. Vernon asked about the debt but did not press; Franklin wrote an honest acknowledgment requesting forbearance, which Vernon granted; later repaid principal with interest, correcting that erratum.
Andrew Hamilton returned from England with a seat in the Assembly and strongly interceded for Franklin's printing appointment, as he did in many subsequent instances until his death.
Meredith's father could advance only 100 pounds of the promised capital; the merchant sued for the remaining 100 pounds and the press was at risk of being sold at half price.
William Coleman and Robert Grace each independently and unsolicited offered to advance all the money needed for Franklin to take the printing business on his own.

Meredith confessed he was not fit for the trade and proposed dissolving the partnership — Franklin to take the debts, repay the 100 pounds, pay personal debts, and give Meredith 30 pounds and a new saddle; the agreement was signed immediately.
Meredith went to North Carolina; sent two long letters the following year describing the country, climate, and soil — Franklin printed them in the papers.
Took half the needed sum from Coleman and half from Grace to avoid showing preference; paid the company's debts and continued the business in his own name circa 1729.

Wrote and printed the anonymous pamphlet 'The Nature and Necessity of a Paper Currency'; well received by common people; weakened wealthy opponents who had no writer to answer it; the House voted more paper money and rewarded Franklin with the contract to print it.
Obtained through Hamilton the contract to print the Newcastle paper money and the laws and votes of that government — held the latter as long as he followed the business.
Opened a stationer's shop with blanks, paper, parchment, and books; hired compositor Whitemash from London and took Aquila Rose's son as apprentice.
Keimer was eventually forced to sell his printing-house to satisfy creditors and left for Barbados in poor circumstances.

David Harry bought Keimer's materials, set up at Philadelphia, rejected a partnership with Franklin, fell into expense and debt, and eventually followed Keimer to Barbados — where the former apprentice employed his former master as a journeyman before both failed.

Bradford kept the post-office and denied Franklin postal distribution of the gazette; Franklin bribed post-riders privately and resolved never to repeat Bradford's practice when he later held the position.
Boarded with Thomas Godfrey; Mrs. Godfrey arranged a courtship with a relation's daughter but the family broke it off after Bradford told them the printing business was unprofitable.
Suspected the Godfreys of maneuvering toward a secret marriage and resolved to have nothing more to do with that family; the Godfreys removed from the house, leaving it entirely to Franklin.

Thought marriage prospects poor because printers were thought a low trade; in the meantime fell into intrigues with low women, attended with expense and risk to health from venereal distemper — escaped by good luck.

Renewed mutual affection with Deborah Read; despite obstacles (her marriage to Rogers possibly still valid, his debts), married her on 1 September 1730 — correcting the great London erratum of neglect.
Proposed to the Junto that members pool their books in a shared room at Grace's; after a year the collection was separated due to careless handling.

Drew up proposals for a public subscription library, had them put in form by scrivener Brockden, and secured fifty subscribers of 40 shillings each for fifty years — the mother of all North American subscription libraries.
Resumed writing the autobiography at Passy, near Paris, in 1784, having been too busy until then to comply with the James and Vaughan letters urging continuation.
Learned by experience that presenting oneself as the proposer of a public project provoked reluctance; thereafter always put himself out of sight and attributed proposals to 'a number of friends.'

Found his China bowl and silver spoon at breakfast one morning — bought by Deborah without his knowledge for 23 shillings; the first plate and china in the house, eventually growing to several hundred pounds in value.

Attended the Presbyterian meeting five Sundays successively at the minister's urging; found the sermons polemic and unedifying — aimed at making Presbyterians not good citizens — and stopped attending.
Conceived the project of arriving at moral perfection and devised a list of thirteen virtues with precepts, planning to work through them methodically.
Began executing the thirteen-virtue self-examination plan — surprised to find himself fuller of faults than imagined, but had the satisfaction of seeing them diminish.

Transferred the virtue-tracking book from paper (which became full of holes from scraping) to ivory memorandum leaves with red ink lines, marking faults with a black-lead pencil wiped with a wet sponge.

Over time reduced the virtue-examination course from weekly through all thirteen, to once a year, then once every several years, then omitted entirely when voyages and multiplying affairs interfered — but always carried the little book.
Noted in a library memorandum dated May 19, 1731 that most public affairs are driven by party interest, not benevolence — first recorded rise of the United Party for Virtue concept.
Wrote at home in August 1788, resuming the autobiography after the Passy section, noting many papers were lost in the war.

The United Party for Virtue project was communicated in part to two young men who adopted it with enthusiasm, but was never further prosecuted — postponed indefinitely due to narrow circumstances and multiplying public and private occupations.
In 1732 published the first Poor Richard's Almanac under the name Richard Saunders, continuing it for about twenty-five years with annual sales near ten thousand copies.

In 1757 assembled the scattered almanac proverbs into a connected discourse — the harangue of Father Abraham — prefixed to the Almanac of 1757; it was copied across the continent, reprinted in Britain, translated twice into French, and distributed by clergy and gentry to the poor.

Sent a journeyman to Charleston, South Carolina around 1733 with a press and letters on a one-third-profit partnership; the journeyman gave poor accounts but his Dutch widow proved an exemplary business partner and eventually bought the printing-house.

Around 1734 championed the preacher Hemphill against the orthodox Presbyterian synod, writing two or three pamphlets and a Gazette piece in his defence; the cause was defeated when Hemphill's sermons were exposed as plagiarized from Dr. Foster.
In 1733 began studying languages — acquired French, then Italian (using chess games as a language-learning incentive), then Spanish; later found these smoothed recovery of Latin.
After ten years' absence, visited Boston and Newport — met brother James, whose illness was advanced; agreed to take James's ten-year-old son and raise him in the printing business.

In 1736 lost a four-year-old son to smallpox contracted in the common way — bitterly regretted not having given it by inoculation, a standing regret urged on other parents as reason to choose inoculation.
In 1736 was chosen clerk of the General Assembly — won over a wealthy opponent who had spoken against him by borrowing a rare book from his library, turning an adversary into a lasting friend.
In 1737 Colonel Spotswood offered Franklin the Philadelphia postmaster-general deputyship — accepted; it greatly improved newspaper correspondence and profits while Bradford's rival paper declined.
Proposed in Junto to form five or six subordinate clubs (Vine, Union, Band, etc.) rather than expanding Junto membership — used these clubs to spread Junto sentiments and influence public opinion.

Wrote a Junto paper on city watch reform — proposed hired professional watch and proportional property tax instead of the flat six-shilling constable fee; idea paved the way for a law several years later.
Wrote a Junto paper on fire prevention and carelessness — it gave rise to the formation of the Union Fire Company, with thirty associates pledged to keep leather buckets and baskets and meet monthly.

In 1739 Reverend Whitefield arrived in Philadelphia from Ireland — crowds so large the clergy refused him pulpits; a multi-denominational meetinghouse was built expressly to host any preacher of any persuasion.

Attended a Whitefield sermon he had resolved not to contribute to — was progressively moved by the oratory to empty his entire pocket (copper, silver, and five gold pistoles) into the collection dish.
Printed Whitefield's sermons and journals over the years — was intimately acquainted with him and testified unreservedly to his integrity despite accusations of misappropriating collections.
Measured Whitefield's voice reach by walking back toward the river during a Market Street sermon — computed he could be heard by over thirty thousand by geometric calculation.
Union Fire Company still subsisted and flourished at the time of writing — over fifty years since founding — with all original members deceased but Franklin and one man older than him.

Printing partnerships extended to other colonies — promoted well-behaved workmen by establishing them in printing-houses on six-year terms, after which they purchased the types and worked for themselves; all partnerships ended amicably.
In 1743 drew up a proposal for a Philadelphia academy; the intended superintendent Mr. Peters declined in favour of more profitable service to the proprietaries; scheme lay dormant.
In 1744 proposed and established the American Philosophical Society.

Wrote and published Plain Truth pamphlet in the mid-1740s on Pennsylvania's defenceless state; within days over twelve hundred signed in Philadelphia and ultimately over ten thousand across the province.
Officers of the Philadelphia regiment chose Franklin as colonel; he declined and recommended Mr. Lawrence instead, then organized a lottery to build a river battery and procure cannon.

Sent to New York with Colonel Lawrence, William Allen, and Abram Taylor to borrow cannon from Governor Clinton — Clinton softened over dinner and Madeira wine from a flat refusal to lending eighteen eighteen-pound cannon with carriages.

Drafted the province's first fast-day proclamation (drawing on New England practice) — translated into German and printed in both languages; used the clergy of all sects to promote the defense association.
Warned that his defense activity might cost him the Assembly clerkship — responded he would never ask, refuse, nor resign an office; was re-elected unanimously at the next election.

Eight Quaker fire-company members stationed at a nearby tavern offered to come vote for the battery lottery if needed — their hidden support secured the majority without their having to appear; the measure passed eight to one.

In 1742 invented an open stove for warming rooms and saving fuel — gave the model to Robert Grace for his iron furnace; wrote a pamphlet promoting it; declined Governor Thomas's patent offer on principle.

After peace ended the association, revived the academy scheme — assembled active friends (many from Junto), published the Proposals Relating to the Education of Youth, and raised a five-thousand-pound subscription payable in five annual quotas.
In 1749 Franklin and attorney-general Mr. Francis drew up constitutions for the academy; a house was hired, masters engaged, and schools opened.

Negotiated the transfer of the Whitefield building to the academy trustees — brokered the deal to discharge the building's debts, preserve a hall for preachers, and maintain a free school for poor children.
Took David Hall as printing partner circa 1748 — Hall managed all printing-office operations and paid Franklin his share of profits for eighteen years.
Academy trustees incorporated by governor's charter; funds increased by British contributions and proprietary land grants; the institution became the University of Philadelphia.

After retiring from private business Franklin was appointed to the commission of the peace, chosen to the common council, made alderman, and elected burgess to the Assembly — all spontaneously and unsolicited.
Withdrew gradually from the justice-of-the-peace bench, finding his common-law knowledge insufficient to act with credit.
Franklin and Speaker Norris were commissioned as treaty commissioners and went to Carlisle to meet the Indians.
At Carlisle, Franklin and Norris forbade liquor sales during the treaty; upon its successful conclusion gave the Indians rum, which produced a drunken, disorderly scene that evening.

In 1751 Dr. Thomas Bond conceived the Pennsylvania Hospital for the poor sick; Franklin championed it by writing newspaper pieces and procuring subscriptions after Bond told him no project moved without Franklin's involvement.
Purchased Dr. Spence's electrical apparatus and began electrical experiments with great alacrity after retiring from private business.

Drew a conditional hospital bill — matching public gift of 2,000 pounds if private subscriptions reached a set capital — which passed the Assembly and secured funding to erect the Pennsylvania Hospital building.

Declined to solicit for Rev. Gilbert Tennent's Arch-street meetinghouse but gave him practical fundraising advice — ask everyone, including those you expect to refuse — and Tennent raised a larger sum than anticipated.
Helped get a block of Philadelphia market street paved with stone and arranged a sixpence-per-month neighborhood sweeper — unanimously signed — which sparked a city-wide desire for paving.
Drew a bill for paving the city and brought it into the Assembly just before leaving for England in 1757; the bill passed after he left, with street-lighting added.
Improved Philadelphia street-lamp design — replacing globe lamps with four flat panes and a funnel with air crevices to keep them clean and bright through the night.
In London proposed a pre-rain street-sweeping system to Dr. Fothergill — noting that dry-weather sweeping prevented the greater labor of mud-raking.

Craven-street Fothergill street-sweeping anecdote — found a poor feeble woman sweeping his pavement for alms; paid her a shilling to sweep the whole street; servant confirmed it was perfectly clean in three hours.
Appointed joint Postmaster General of America with William Hunter in 1753 — the office was initially 900 pounds in debt to them over four years before turning profitable.
In 1753 Harvard (College of Cambridge) conferred on Franklin the degree of Master of Arts on their own motion; Yale had done the same before — both in recognition of electrical discoveries.
In 1754 served as Pennsylvania commissioner at the Albany Congress to treat with the Six Nations — projected and presented his Plan of Union, which was unanimously adopted by the Congress.
The Albany Plan was rejected by the colonial assemblies (too much prerogative) and by England (too democratic) — the Board of Trade adopted a governor-and-council scheme instead.
Discussed the Albany Plan with Governor Shirley in Boston the winter of 1754-5 — concluded the contrary reasons for rejection suggested the plan was the true medium.
The Pennsylvania Assembly reprobated the Albany Plan without attention while Franklin was absent — to his no small mortification.
Met new Governor Morris in New York — Morris promised to avoid Assembly disputes but was already in contention with them by the time Franklin returned from Boston.
Put on every Assembly committee to draft answers to Governor Morris's messages — the replies often tart and abusive, yet Franklin and Morris dined together personally without rift.
Suggested using Loan Office orders payable in a year at 5% interest to fund the Crown Point aid — the Assembly adopted the plan, the orders were eagerly bought up, and Mr. Quincy returned thanks.
Visited General Braddock at Fredericktown as postmaster-general — removed his prejudices against the Assembly; learned the expedition had only 25 usable wagons when 150 were needed.
At Braddock's suggestion, published an advertisement at Lancaster on April 26, 1755 and a companion address to the back-county inhabitants — procured 150 wagons and 259 horses within two weeks.
Gave personal bond to wagon owners for payment in case of loss, after they distrusted Braddock's promise — advanced over 200 pounds of his own money beyond the 800 pounds received from the general.

Wrote to the Assembly committee warmly recommending relief for Dunbar's regiment subalterns — procured 20 parcels of necessaries conducted by his son to camp, received with great thanks from both colonels.

Advanced over 1,000 pounds sterling of his own money for Braddock's provisions — Braddock returned 1,000 pounds by order on the paymaster a few days before his defeat; the remainder was never recovered.
Warned Braddock of ambush danger from Indians on his long narrow line of march — Braddock smiled at his ignorance; the defeat followed exactly as feared.
Braddock's army was defeated at Fort Duquesne — 63 of 86 officers killed or wounded, 714 of 1100 men killed; all wagons, artillery, and stores lost to the enemy.
After Braddock's defeat, wagon owners sued Franklin on his bond — Shirley eventually appointed commissioners to examine claims of nearly 20,000 pounds, relieving Franklin from potential ruin.
Declined to support the Bond brothers' firework-rejoicing subscription before Braddock's return — predicted uncertainty of war events; the subscription was dropped.

After Braddock's defeat, Governor Morris redoubled Assembly pressure for defense bills — Assembly held firm against proprietary estate exemptions; news reaching England caused proprietaries to add 5,000 pounds of their own money.
The Assembly accepted the proprietaries' contribution in lieu of a general tax; a new bill with an exempting clause for Quakers passed, appropriating sixty thousand pounds for defense.
Drew and carried through the Assembly a voluntary militia bill leaving Quakers at liberty, then wrote a dialogue answering objections to the militia.
Appointed one of the commissioners for disposing of sixty thousand pounds appropriated for defense by the Assembly.
Took charge of the north-western frontier with full commission from the governor — raised five hundred sixty men with his son William as aide-de-camp.
Assembled companies at Bethlehem and was surprised to find the Moravian settlement already well defended — stockades, arms from New York, and paving stones for the women to throw.
Sent detachments toward the Minisink and lower frontier; marched with the rest to Gnadenhut where the Indians had burned and massacred the inhabitants.
Gave guns to eleven farmers who wanted to retrieve their cattle; Indians met them on the road and killed ten — their guns having been wetted by rain.
Built a palisade fort at Gnadenhut in a week — four hundred fifty-five foot circumference, seventy axes, carriages improvised from wagon wheels — despite rain on alternate days.
Scouting parties found no Indians but discovered their concealed hillside fire-holes — coals from burnt logs burned in pits with men lying round, feet hanging in to keep warm.
Chaplain Beatty complained of poor prayer attendance; Franklin suggested he deal out the daily rum ration just after prayers — attendance immediately became perfectly regular.
Recalled by the governor for the Assembly session after completing three forts; handed command to Colonel Clapham and returned, resting at Bethlehem before the journey.

Observed the Moravian commune at Bethlehem — common stock, common tables, dormitories with ventilation loopholes, and segregated church services by age and sex; children looked pale from too little exercise.
Returned to Philadelphia and accepted the colonelcy of the militia regiment — twelve hundred men with an artillery company expert enough to fire twelve rounds a minute.
Commission broken when English Parliament repealed the militia law; the regiment's escort of Franklin out of town with drawn swords greatly offended the proprietor.
Proprietor accused Franklin to the ministry of obstructing the king's service and applied to postmaster-general Fawkener to remove him from office — Fawkener gave only a gentle admonition.
Met Dr. Spence in Boston in 1746 who showed imperfect electrical experiments — returned to Philadelphia eager to repeat and extend them with the Collinson glass tube.

Wrote several letters to Collinson on electrical experiments; they were read at the Royal Society but initially not printed in their Transactions — the lightning-sameness paper was laughed at by the connoisseurs.

Dr. Fothergill rescued the electrical papers — deemed too valuable to suppress, they were given to Cave, printed separately as a pamphlet with Fothergill's preface, and eventually swelled to a quarto volume with five editions.
Encouraged neighbor Kinnersley to exhibit electrical experiments for money — wrote him two ordered lectures that he toured through every colonial capital and the West Indies.

Buffon had Dalibard translate Franklin's electrical papers into French; they were printed at Paris and drew the hostile attention of Abbé Nollet, who published a volume of letters denying Franklin's experiments.

Declined to answer Nollet — concluded it was better to make new experiments than dispute about old ones; M. le Roy of the Royal Academy eventually refuted Nollet; Franklin's book was translated into Italian, German, and Latin.
Dalibard and De Lor performed the Marly lightning-from-clouds experiment before the French king and court — making the Philadelphia Experiments famous throughout Europe.
Performed the kite experiment in Philadelphia — drawing lightning from clouds; both experiments recorded in histories of electricity.
Elected a Fellow of the Royal Society without application and excused the customary payments of twenty-five guineas; thereafter received the Transactions gratis.
Awarded the Copley Gold Medal for 1753 by the Royal Society — presented with a handsome speech by Lord Macclesfield.

Governor Denny delivered the Copley Medal and privately offered Franklin implied rewards if he would moderate his Assembly opposition — Franklin rebuffed the overture, pledging only to support measures good for the people.
Assembly appointed Franklin their agent to go to England to petition the king against proprietary instructions; he booked passage with Captain Morris at New York.

Lord Loudoun arrived in Philadelphia to mediate between governor and Assembly; heard both sides but ultimately pressed the Assembly to comply rather than advise the governor to override his instructions.
Presented Assembly resolutions declaring rights suspended only under force — the bill was reframed to conform with proprietary instructions; Franklin was then free to depart for England.
Detained at New York from early April to near the end of June 1757 by Lord Loudoun's chronic indecision — three packet-boats held waiting for letters that were always 'ready tomorrow.'

Sailed with Loudoun's fleet toward Louisbourg — freed after five days with a dispatch; the ship steered for England while Loudoun took the other packets to Halifax and returned to New York without besieging anything.

Presented Braddock provisions accounts to Lord Loudoun at New York — certified correct, but Loudoun refused to pay, saying Franklin should apply to the Treasury in England; the balance remains unpaid.
Crossed to England in thirty days — the ship proved slow until cargo was redistributed aft; Captain Kennedy lost a wager on the ship's thirteen-knot speed.
Near-shipwreck at midnight approaching Falmouth — almost struck rocks at the lighthouse; Captain Kennedy ordered the ship to wear round with all sails standing, carrying them clear.
Arrived in London July 27 1757 — stopped at Stonehenge and Wilton on the way from Falmouth; settled in lodgings Mr. Charles had arranged.

Met Lord Granville the day after arriving — Granville asserted that the king is the legislator of the colonies and his instructions are law; Franklin disputed it and recorded the conversation immediately.
Met proprietaries at T. Penn's Spring Garden house — talks quickly revealed wide disagreement; Franklin submitted written complaints, but they were handed to Paris who sat on them for nearly a year.

Governor Denny passed the act taxing the proprietary estate — the grand point of the dispute — making the proprietaries' Assembly message moot; they then petitioned the king in Council to block the act.

A hearing before the king in Council on the proprietary tax act — two lawyers each side; Lord Mansfield privately asked Franklin to assure the proprietary estate would not be injured, then brokered a written engagement that allowed the law to pass.
Assembly assessed with perfect equity under the tax act — a committee including proprietary friends unanimously confirmed fairness; the Assembly thanked Franklin formally on his return.
Governor Denny was turned out by the proprietaries and threatened with suit for breach of instructions; he despised the threats (having acted for the General's service) and they were never executed.

communication.label: Communication style
communication.line: How they like to be spoken to.

life.label: Life
life.line: Boston origins, rise through Philadelphia, first London printing-house stay, and second London diplomatic mission — the arc of a life that also includes deep personal losses in Philadelphia and the late autobiography revival at Passy and home.

life/autobiography.label: Autobiography writing
life/autobiography.line: Autobiography written in three bursts — first section to Deborah's time, resumed at Passy in 1784 after James and Vaughan letters urged continuation, resumed again at home in August 1788 with many papers lost in the war.

life/london.label: London stay
life/london.line: London (Dec 1724, ~18 months) — worked at Palmer's then Watts's, earned 'Water-American' nickname, reformed chapel laws, befriended Hamilton and Denham, swam the Thames, sold Sloane an asbestos purse; left owing 27 pounds from Ralph; a formative if financially imprudent period.

life/london-second.label: Second London stay
life/london-second.line: Arrived London July 27 1757 as Assembly agent — lodged via Mr. Charles; immediately consulted Fothergill on tactics, met Collinson, was introduced to Lord Granville; negotiations with proprietaries at Penn's Spring Garden house went nowhere for over a year.

life/origins.label: Origins and ancestry
life/origins.line: Born the youngest son in Boston to a long line of English Nonconformist smiths; rose from obscurity through voracious reading and natural leadership, with formal schooling cut short by family circumstance.

life/origins/ancestry.label: Family ancestry
life/origins/ancestry.line: Centuries-old Protestant smithing family from Ecton, Northamptonshire — Nonconformists who emigrated to Boston; Franklin is their youngest son.

life/origins/boyhood.label: Boyhood and early education
life/origins/boyhood.line: Boyhood in Boston — voracious self-taught reader, natural leader among boys, swimmer and boat-handler; built prose style from the Spectator, read widely in philosophy and navigation, and briefly adopted then abandoned a vegetarian diet.

life/philadelphia.label: Philadelphia
life/philadelphia.line: Arrived as a penniless, ragged seventeen-year-old; went on to make a considerable figure there — the city of his rise.

money.label: Money
money.line: Early finances marked by errata (Vernon, Collins, Ralph) — Vernon debt repaid with interest; Braddock provisions advanced at great personal risk, partially recovered, balance still owed; Denham's modest salary; Deborah's china bowl the first household luxury.

money-style.label: Money style
money-style.line: How they handle money: discipline, risk, planning.

people.label: People
people.line: The full cast of Franklin's life — family who formed him, patrons who proved unreliable or faithful, Philadelphia friends and business partners who shaped his career, civic allies who backed his projects, and British commanders and legal figures encountered in public life; several relationships carry standing regret or deep loss, while a few — Coleman, Denham, Hall — proved steady anchors.

people/abbe-nollet.label: Abbé Nollet
people/abbe-nollet.line: French natural philosopher and royal preceptor whose electricity theory Franklin's experiments overturned — attacked Franklin in a volume of letters but Franklin declined to answer, letting his experiments speak for themselves; Nollet ended as the last of his sect.

people/abiah-folger.label: Abiah Folger Franklin
people/abiah-folger.line: Mother — robust constitution, suckled all ten children, died at 85; buried with Josiah in Boston under a stone Franklin placed.

people/andrew-hamilton.label: Andrew Hamilton
people/andrew-hamilton.line: Philadelphia lawyer and Assembly member — introduced Franklin to Governor Keith, returned from England with a seat in the House, and strongly supported Franklin's printing appointments; continued his patronage until his death.

people/beatty.label: Rev. Beatty
people/beatty.line: Zealous Presbyterian chaplain on the frontier — persuaded by Franklin to distribute rum after prayers, which solved the attendance problem instantly.

people/charles-osborne.label: Charles Osborne
people/charles-osborne.line: Philadelphia friend — sensible, candid, and frank; too fond of criticising in literary matters; went to the West Indies, became an eminent lawyer, died young; had a pact with Franklin to visit after death but never fulfilled it.

people/david-hall.label: David Hall
people/david-hall.line: Able, industrious, honest printing partner from 1748 — worked four years for Franklin before taking over the printing office; paid punctually for eighteen successful years.

people/deborah-read.label: Deborah Read
people/deborah-read.line: Wife from September 1730 — first seen on Franklin's ragged Philadelphia arrival; her unhappy first marriage to Rogers the potter was partly caused by Franklin's London inconstancy, which he regarded as the great erratum; she proved a good and faithful helpmate who attended the shop; they throve together.

people/dr-fothergill.label: Dr. Fothergill
people/dr-fothergill.line: London physician and great promoter of useful projects — among the best men Franklin had known; rescued Franklin's electrical papers from suppression and wrote the preface for their publication.

people/family.label: Family
people/family.line: Franklin's immediate family: a formative father, a devoted mother, a tyrannical older brother who forged his aversion to arbitrary power, a loving brother in Newport, and an ingenious uncle who taught him shorthand.

people/ferdinand-paris.label: Ferdinand John Paris
people/ferdinand-paris.line: Proprietary solicitor — proud and angry man with a mortal enmity to Franklin; managed all the proprietaries' legal disputes and drew their Assembly messages; Franklin refused to deal through him and insisted on treating only with the proprietaries themselves.

people/general-braddock.label: General Braddock
people/general-braddock.line: British commander met at Fredericktown — overconfident, dismissed Indian allies, ignored Franklin's ambush warning; his defeat proved catastrophic and left Franklin holding a nearly ruinous 20,000-pound wagon bond.

people/general-shirley.label: General Shirley
people/general-shirley.line: British general who succeeded Braddock as army commander — sensible, sagacious, and attentive to good advice; Franklin regarded him as far more capable than Loudoun, and was sincerely glad when relieved of the burdensome command.

people/george-webb.label: George Webb
people/george-webb.line: Oxford scholar who bought out his Keimer indenture with a female friend's help, then betrayed Franklin's newspaper plan to Keimer — a foolish confidence Franklin regretted.

people/gilbert-tennent.label: Rev. Gilbert Tennent
people/gilbert-tennent.line: Presbyterian minister who sought Franklin's help for a subscription meetinghouse — Franklin declined to solicit but gave cannily practical fundraising advice that yielded Tennent a larger sum than expected.

people/governor-burnet.label: Governor Burnet of New York
people/governor-burnet.line: Governor of New York, son of Bishop Burnet — summoned Franklin on hearing he carried many books; showed him a large library; the second governor to honor Franklin with notice.

people/governor-denny.label: Captain Denny
people/governor-denny.line: New governor who succeeded Morris — delivered the Copley Medal to Franklin, sought his goodwill with flattery and implied rewards, but remained hampered by proprietary instructions; personally pleasant, a man of letters who informed Franklin that James Ralph was prosperous in England.

people/governor-keith.label: Governor Sir William Keith
people/governor-keith.line: Governor of Pennsylvania — warmly patronized Franklin with promises of a printing-house setup in England; sent no letters and had no credit to give — a habit of pleasing with expectations he could never deliver; Franklin's credulity a standing regret.

people/governor-morris.label: Governor Morris
people/governor-morris.line: Governor of Pennsylvania — an intimate acquaintance, eloquent and an acute sophister who loved disputing; promised Franklin to avoid Assembly quarrels but fell into constant contention with them; no personal rift with Franklin despite the public battle.

people/hemphill.label: Hemphill
people/hemphill.line: Young Irish Presbyterian preacher arrived 1734 — excellent sermons, which Franklin championed; later discovered to be plagiarized from Dr. Foster; his cause defeated at synod; Franklin stuck by him but quitted the congregation after.

people/hugh-meredith.label: Hugh Meredith
people/hugh-meredith.line: Welsh Pennsylvanian, honest but given to drink — proposed the printing partnership and his father furnished the capital; unable to deliver the full sum, he dissolved the partnership circa 1729 and went to farm in North Carolina.

people/james-franklin.label: James Franklin
people/james-franklin.line: Older brother and master printer — frequently beat Franklin in passion; the strained apprenticeship ended in secret escape; later reconciled warmly at Newport where James was dying, entrusting his son to Franklin's care.

people/james-franklin-jr.label: James Franklin Jr.
people/james-franklin-jr.line: Son of James — taken into Franklin's care per his brother's deathbed request; sent to school then trained in printing; later assisted with new types when his father's worn out; Franklin's care seen as amends for leaving James early.

people/james-logan.label: James Logan
people/james-logan.line: Honorable Quaker scholar, former secretary to William Penn — supported defensive war, gave sixty pounds for the battery lottery, and shared the anecdote of Penn rebuking him for staying on deck during a naval scare.

people/james-ralph.label: James Ralph
people/james-ralph.line: Philadelphia friend — eloquent, borrowed freely, deserted his wife for England; ended the friendship when Franklin attempted liberties with Mrs. T; the debt was never repaid; later learned Ralph became a respected political writer in England with a pension of 300 pounds, though Pope damned his poetry.

people/john-collins.label: John Collins
people/john-collins.line: Boyhood friend and mathematical genius — helped Franklin escape Boston; later fell into daily drunkenness and gambling, borrowed heavily from Vernon's money Franklin held, then vanished to Barbados — a standing loss and financial regret.

people/john-franklin.label: John Franklin
people/john-franklin.line: Older brother, married and settled in Newport — always loved Franklin and received him warmly.

people/joseph-watson.label: Joseph Watson
people/joseph-watson.line: Philadelphia friend — pious, sensible, of great integrity; the best of the set; died in Franklin's arms a few years later, much lamented.

people/josiah-franklin.label: Josiah Franklin
people/josiah-franklin.line: Father — tallow-chandler in Boston, a prudent and pious man consulted as arbitrator by neighbors; deeply formative — corrected Franklin's ethics and shaped his indifference to food.

people/junto-members.label: Junto members
people/junto-members.line: Core members of the Junto club — mutual-improvement companions who recommended business, contributed queries, and debated morals, politics, and natural philosophy on Friday evenings.

people/keimer.label: Samuel Keimer
people/keimer.line: Philadelphia printer who employed Franklin twice, was easily duped, grew captious, and eventually failed — sold his press to creditors, went to Barbados in poverty, and died there after his apprentice Harry briefly employed him as a journeyman.

people/kinnersley.label: Ebenezer Kinnersley
people/kinnersley.line: Ingenious neighbor Franklin encouraged to make a living exhibiting electrical experiments — Franklin wrote him two lectures, Kinnersley toured the colonies and West Indies with them.

people/lord-granville.label: Lord Granville
people/lord-granville.line: President of the Council — met Franklin soon after his London arrival and asserted the alarming doctrine that the king is the sole legislator of the colonies; Franklin disputed this but was alarmed enough to write the conversation down immediately.

people/lord-loudoun.label: Lord Loudoun
people/lord-loudoun.line: British commander whose chronic indecision detained packet-boats for months — his 1757 campaign was disgraceful and ineffective; refused to pay Franklin's certified Braddock accounts, leaving a standing debt; removed by Pitt in favor of Amherst and Wolfe.

people/lord-mansfield.label: Lord Mansfield
people/lord-mansfield.line: Counsel in the proprietary tax hearing — privately brokered the compromise that saved the Pennsylvania tax act; asked Franklin if he would personally assure the proprietary estate would not be injured, then brought Paris in to seal the agreement.

people/michael-welfare.label: Michael Welfare
people/michael-welfare.line: Founder of the Dunkers sect — acquainted with Franklin; shared his sect's reason for not publishing a confession of faith: their principles were still improving and they feared being bound by a fixed creed.

people/mr-denham.label: Mr. Denham
people/mr-denham.line: Quaker merchant of exemplary integrity — repaid Bristol creditors in full from American fortune; brought Franklin back from London as his clerk; counselled him like a father; died in early 1727 leaving a small legacy — Franklin's most reliable patron, a deep loss.

people/patrons.label: Patrons and employers
people/patrons.line: Patrons and employers of Franklin's early career — Governor Keith promised much and delivered nothing (a standing credulity regret); Keimer employed him but was easily duped; Bradford sent him onward; Burnet honored him.

people/peter-collinson.label: Peter Collinson
people/peter-collinson.line: Fellow of the Royal Society who sent the Library Company a glass tube that launched Franklin's electrical experiments — got Franklin's experiment letters read at the Royal Society, and eventually gave them to Cave for publication.

people/philadelphia-friends.label: Philadelphia friends
people/philadelphia-friends.line: Franklin's Philadelphia literary circle — Ralph (eloquent, deserted wife for England), Osborne (candid critic, died young with a broken pact), Watson (pious, best of the set, died in Franklin's arms), and Denham (Quaker merchant whose friendship lasted his life).

people/quincy.label: Mr. Quincy
people/quincy.line: Massachusetts envoy who sought Pennsylvania aid for the Crown Point attack — Franklin dictated his address to the Assembly; Quincy returned home well pleased and bore Franklin cordial lifelong friendship.

people/robert-holmes.label: Robert Holmes
people/robert-holmes.line: Brother-in-law — master of a sloop trading between Boston and Delaware; told Governor Keith of Franklin's abilities, inadvertently launching Keith's patronage offer.

people/samuel-mickle.label: Samuel Mickle
people/samuel-mickle.line: Philadelphia pessimist who tried to discourage Franklin at the door of his new printing-house — predicted the city's ruin, refused to buy property for years, and eventually paid five times what he could have for a house.

people/thomas-bond.label: Dr. Thomas Bond
people/thomas-bond.line: Philadelphia physician and particular friend — conceived the Pennsylvania Hospital in 1751; needed Franklin's backing to make subscriptions move.

people/uncle-benjamin.label: Uncle Benjamin Franklin
people/uncle-benjamin.line: Father's brother — silk dyer, ingenious poet and politician; Franklin named after him; taught Franklin his personal shorthand.

people/vernon.label: Mr. Vernon
people/vernon.line: Trusted Franklin with 35 pounds — the debt was a named erratum for years; Franklin eventually repaid principal with interest and was forgiven, correcting the erratum.

people/whitefield.label: George Whitefield
people/whitefield.line: Itinerant preacher of extraordinary oratory — arrived 1739, attracted enormous crowds, inspired the building of a multi-denominational meetinghouse; Franklin printed his sermons and journals; their friendship was civil and sincere, each frank about the religious divide — Whitefield praying for Franklin's conversion, Franklin noting it never took; wholly trusted as honest by Franklin despite accusations of misappropriation.

people/william-bradford.label: William Bradford
people/william-bradford.line: Old printer in New York — first printer in Pennsylvania, removed to New York; could not hire Franklin but sent him to his son in Philadelphia.

people/william-coleman.label: William Coleman
people/william-coleman.line: Junto member and lifelong friend — coolest, clearest head, best heart, exactest morals of almost any man Franklin met; became a merchant of great note and provincial judge; friendship lasted uninterrupted forty-plus years until his death.

temperament.label: Temperament
temperament.line: Industrious, practically minded, and a candid self-aware rationalizer — manages public image of industry and frugality deliberately; lets verifiable work speak rather than disputing; susceptible to eloquence despite resolve; solves human problems with practical incentive design; chooses prudence over rigid principle.

temperament/civic-personality.label: Civic personality
temperament/civic-personality.line: Publicly spirited first mover who suppresses his own visible role to avoid envy — indispensable to every civic project; industrious beyond neighbors; manages frugal public image deliberately; believes one person with a good plan can work great changes; receives offices without solicitation; lets work speak rather than dispute.

temperament/ethics.label: Ethics and values
temperament/ethics.line: Holds virtue to be rational self-interest and honesty its foundation; deeply averse to arbitrary power and tyranny; candid about his own errata and vanity; attributes fortune to providence; freely shares inventions and rewards helpers before self-interest.

temperament/ethics/civic-virtue.label: Civic ethics
temperament/ethics/civic-virtue.line: Opposes arbitrary power and tyranny from deep conviction; uses strategic cunning for public benefit without scruple when ends are good; recommends written partnership articles to prevent quarrels.

temperament/ethics/virtue-doctrine.label: Virtue doctrine
temperament/ethics/virtue-doctrine.line: Frames virtue as rational self-interest — vicious acts forbidden because hurtful, not the reverse; freely shares inventions; places loyalty to helpers above immediate gain; more generous when poor than wealthy.

temperament/expression.label: Expression and argument style
temperament/expression.line: Habitually expresses opinions with modest diffidence — prefers 'I conceive' and 'it appears to me' over positive assertion; practiced the Socratic method for years before moderating to diffident expression.

temperament/religion.label: Religious beliefs
temperament/religion.line: Raised Presbyterian but found the dogmas unintelligible; settled on a private creed of five essentials — Deity's existence, Providence, doing good as the best service to God, immortality of the soul, reward and punishment — respected all religions without attending any publicly; composed his own private liturgy in 1728.

temperament/self-improvement.label: Self-improvement habits
temperament/self-improvement.line: Systematic, methodical self-improver — built prose style from the Spectator, read voraciously, used the library for daily study, kept Sunday as a study day, formed a sea plan of future conduct faithfully observed into old age, and applied the same designed rigor to virtue as to skills.

temperament/virtue-project.label: Moral perfection project
temperament/virtue-project.line: Conceived the bold moral perfection project — thirteen virtues tracked in a ruled book, with a daily schedule and mottos from Addison, Cicero, and Solomon; never reached perfection (Order incorrigible, Pride the most stubborn), but ascribes his long health, early fortune, civic confidence, and cheerful company to the attempt down to his 79th year.
routing: temperance silence order resolution frugality industry sincerity justice moderation cleanliness tranquillity chastity humility

work.label: Work
work.line: Professional and civic career spanning printing, publishing, public office, and invention — built civic institutions across Philadelphia (library, fire company, hospital, academy, defense association), served as Assembly clerk and member, deputy postmaster-general, and electrical discoverer; guided always by the rule of never asking, refusing, or resigning an office.

work/academy.label: Academy proposal
work/academy.line: Philadelphia Academy launched 1749 — Franklin drafted constitutions with Francis, brokered the Whitefield-building transfer, and watched it grow into the University of Philadelphia over forty years as trustee.

work/albany-plan.label: Albany Plan of Union
work/albany-plan.line: Drafted the Albany Plan of Union in 1754 — a colonial union under a crown-appointed president-general and elected grand council; unanimously adopted by the Congress but rejected as too prerogative-heavy by assemblies and too democratic by England.

work/assembly-member.label: Assembly membership
work/assembly-member.line: Ten-year Assembly member never soliciting a vote — began as clerk in 1736, led all proprietary-tax battles and defense legislation, rebuffed Governor Denny's implied rewards, was appointed Assembly agent to England, and returned to formal thanks for securing the proprietary tax act.

work/civic-projects.label: Civic improvement projects
work/civic-projects.line: Began turning thoughts to public affairs in the late 1730s — city watch reform, fire company formation, proposed proportional watch tax — using Junto and subordinate clubs to prepare public opinion and secure eventual legislative success.

work/defense-association.label: Voluntary defense association
work/defense-association.line: Organized Pennsylvania's first voluntary defense association in the mid-1740s — wrote Plain Truth pamphlet, gathered over ten thousand signatures, formed regiments, declined the colonelcy, built a river battery, borrowed cannon from Governor Clinton, and took his own guard duty as a common soldier.

work/electricity.label: Electrical discoveries
work/electricity.line: Began electrical experiments in 1746 after seeing Dr. Spence in Boston — practiced extensively, distributed tubes to friends, discovered lightning equals electricity; papers first laughed at by Royal Society, rescued by Fothergill, eventually published as a quarto volume with five editions.

work/frontier-command.label: Frontier military command
work/frontier-command.line: Commanded five hundred sixty men on the north-western frontier in early 1756 — built three forts including Gnadenhut, observed Indian fire-concealment craft, and returned when the Assembly recalled him.

work/hospital.label: Pennsylvania Hospital
work/hospital.line: Championed Dr. Bond's 1751 hospital proposal — subscribed himself and secured public subscriptions via newspaper preparation; the project had been ascribed to Franklin but originated with Bond.

work/inventions.label: Inventions
work/inventions.line: Invented the Pennsylvania Fireplace in 1742 — gave the model freely to Robert Grace rather than patenting it; declined a governor's patent offer on principle that inventors should serve others freely; others took patents for his inventions without contest.

work/junto.label: Junto club
work/junto.line: Founded the Junto — a Friday-evening mutual-improvement club that Franklin designed with rules suppressing positiveness and requiring written queries and essays; lasted nearly as long as his friendship with Coleman and was the best school of philosophy, morality, and politics in the province.

work/languages.label: Language study
work/languages.line: Began studying French, Italian, Spanish, and Latin in 1733 — self-taught by reading; used a chess game with a condition to learn Italian; later found knowing French, Italian, and Spanish smoothed the way to Latin.

work/library.label: Library Company of Philadelphia
work/library.line: Franklin's first public project — founded the subscription library from a Junto book-pooling experiment; fifty initial subscribers at 40 shillings each; became the mother of all North American subscription libraries.

work/london-agency.label: London agency for Pennsylvania Assembly
work/london-agency.line: Appointed Pennsylvania Assembly's agent to England — navigated Lord Loudoun's delays to sail in 1757; talks with Penn proprietaries stalled for a year; finally secured the proprietary tax act through a compromise brokered by Lord Mansfield; Assembly gave formal thanks on return.

work/philosophical-society.label: American Philosophical Society
work/philosophical-society.line: Proposed and established the American Philosophical Society in 1744 — a learned society for the colonies.

work/poor-richards-almanac.label: Poor Richard's Almanac
work/poor-richards-almanac.line: Published annually under the name Richard Saunders from 1732 for about twenty-five years — sold near ten thousand copies a year; filled with proverbs on industry and frugality; the 1757 preface collected these into The Way to Wealth, widely reprinted and translated.

work/postmaster-general.label: Postmaster General of America
work/postmaster-general.line: Joint Postmaster General of America from 1753 with William Hunter — built the office from zero revenue to three times the yield of the Irish post office before being displaced by a ministerial freak.

work/printing.label: Printing trade
work/printing.line: Printer by trade across four phases — Boston apprentice under James, Philadelphia journeyman at Keimer's (twice), London pressman at Palmer's and Watts's, and independent owner from ~1729; prose writing a principal means of advancement; extended to printing partnerships across multiple colonies on six-year terms, all ending amicably.

work/printing/london.label: London printing work
work/printing/london.line: London printing work — first at Palmer's (nearly a year, wrote Liberty and Necessity pamphlet), then at Watts's; quickly acquired influence, led workmen from beer to water-gruel, earned nickname 'Water-American'.

work/printing/newspaper.label: Newspaper venture
work/printing/newspaper.line: Acquired Keimer's failed Pennsylvania Gazette and built it into an extremely profitable paper — founding it on better type, sharp writing, and the Busy Body campaign that outmaneuvered Keimer's rival proposal.

work/printing/own-shop.label: Own printing shop
work/printing/own-shop.line: Franklin's solo printing shop from ~1729 — survived the Meredith capital crisis thanks to Coleman and Grace, won Assembly and Newcastle printing contracts via Hamilton, printed the paper-currency pamphlet that secured him a profitable monopoly, and grew while every competitor failed; industry visibly shown and frugality publicly performed were the engine.
routing: nature and necessity of a paper currency

work/printing/stationery-shop.label: Stationer's shop
work/printing/stationery-shop.line: Opened a small stationer's shop alongside the printing business — sold blanks, paper, parchment, and books; built reputation for the correctest blanks in the province.

work/united-party-for-virtue.label: United Party for Virtue
work/united-party-for-virtue.line: Conceived a grand secret society — the Society of the Free and Easy — to unite virtuous men of all nations; planned but never fully executed; connected to the Art of Virtue book project.
routing: society of the free and easy

abel-james-letter.text: Abel James sent a letter from Paris urging Franklin to complete and publish his autobiography, enclosing notes Franklin had written up to 1730 — arguing the work would improve industry and temperance in American youth.

abiah-death-age.text: Abiah Franklin died at age 85, born 1667.

academy-no-sect-trustee.text: Franklin was chosen trustee of the Whitefield building trustees because he was regarded as 'merely an honest man, and of no sect at all.'

academy-opened-1749.text: The Philadelphia academy schools opened in 1749 — constitutions drawn by Franklin and attorney-general Francis, house hired, masters engaged.

academy-proposed-peters-declined.text: After peace, revived the academy plan — published Proposals Relating to the Education of Youth and raised a five-thousand-pound subscription in five annual quotas.

history.value: Proposed a Philadelphia academy in 1743; Mr. Peters declined the superintendency in favour of proprietary service; scheme lay dormant.

academy-whitefield-building.text: The academy acquired the Whitefield meetinghouse building — Franklin brokered a deal discharging its debts and preserving a hall for preachers and a free school for poor children.

albany-plan-drafted.text: Drafted a plan for union of all colonies under a crown-appointed president-general and a grand council elected by colonial assemblies — shown to James Alexander and Kennedy in New York who approved it.

albany-plan-rejected.text: The Albany Plan was unanimously adopted by the Congress but rejected by colonial assemblies (too much prerogative) and disapproved by the Board of Trade (too democratic).

albany-plan-would-have-prevented-revolut.text: Still believed that if the Albany Plan had been adopted, the colonies could have defended themselves, removing the pretext for British taxation and the Revolutionary War.

apprenticeship-james-age.text: Apprenticed to brother James at age twelve; indentures ran until age twenty-one with journeyman wages in the final year.

arrived-london-1757.text: Arrived in London July 27 1757 as the Assembly's agent — lodged through Mr. Charles; immediately visited Fothergill for counsel and Collinson for introductions.

art-of-virtue-book-planned.text: Planned a book called The Art of Virtue to explain how virtue benefits the practitioner, showing means not merely urging goodness — never completed due to private and public business demands.

art-of-virtue-doctrine.text: Intended the Art of Virtue to argue that vicious actions are forbidden because they are hurtful — not hurtful because forbidden — and that virtue is in everyone's rational self-interest.

assembly-agent-england.text: Appointed Pennsylvania Assembly's agent to England to petition the king against proprietary instructions — the genesis of his extended London diplomatic mission.

assembly-clerk-1736.text: Chosen clerk of the General Assembly in 1736 — secured printing contracts for votes, laws, paper money, and public jobs; won a resistant wealthy new member's friendship by borrowing a rare book.

assembly-member-elected.text: Elected burgess to the Pennsylvania Assembly in the early 1750s — re-elected every year for ten years without ever asking any elector for his vote.

assembly-printer-appointment.text: The Assembly voted Franklin and Meredith their printers for the ensuing year, after Franklin reprinted the House's address to the governor elegantly, contrasting Bradford's coarse version.

assembly-reprobated-albany-plan.text: The Pennsylvania Assembly took up and reprobated the Albany Plan without attention while Franklin was absent — managed by a certain member — causing him no small mortification.

assembly-thanked-franklin.text: The Assembly gave Franklin formal thanks on his return — regarding his engagement in the Mansfield compromise as an essential service that secured the credit of the paper money spread across the country.

autobiography-resumed-passy-1784.text: Resumed the autobiography at Passy, near Paris, in 1784 — without papers to aid memory, acknowledging dates may need correction when he returned home.

averse-assuming-state.text: Naturally averse to assuming state or pomp on any occasion — was chagrined when officers escorted him with drawn swords without prior notice.

aversion-arbitrary-power.text: Deeply averse to arbitrary power and tyrannical authority.

nudges.note: Explicitly attributed his lifelong aversion to arbitrary power to James's harsh treatment during the apprenticeship.

aversion-to-arbitrary-power.text: James's harsh, tyrannical treatment left a lasting aversion to arbitrary power.

avid-reader-learner.text: Avid reader who spends freely on books and values learning above other pleasures.

nudges.note: Every bit of spare money in childhood went to books; read Plutarch abundantly and still values that time.
Sat up reading borrowed books all night; negotiated board savings expressly to buy more books; taught himself arithmetic, navigation, rhetoric, and Socratic method.

beatty-rum-prayer.text: Advised Chaplain Beatty to deal out the men's rum ration just after prayers — the scheme worked perfectly and prayers were never better attended.

birth-order.text: Youngest son and youngest child but two in a family of seventeen children.

book-borrowing-tactic.text: Turned an adversary (a wealthy Assembly member who had spoken against him) into a lasting friend by requesting to borrow a rare book — illustrating the maxim that one who has done a kindness is readier to repeat it.

braddock-ambush-warning.text: Warned Braddock of Indian ambush risk along the long narrow line of march — Braddock dismissed it; the army was attacked from behind trees exactly as feared, causing a catastrophic rout.

braddock-money-advanced-lost.text: Advanced over 1,000 pounds sterling of his own money for Braddock's provisions — recovered 1,000 pounds by lucky timing before the battle; the remainder was never obtained.

braddock-personal-bond.text: Gave personal bond to wagon owners for payment in case of loss, and advanced over 200 pounds of his own money beyond what Braddock provided.

braddock-recommended-franklin.text: Braddock's letters to the ministry, captured and published by the French, spoke highly of Franklin's service to the army — confirmed later by David Hume; but the expedition's failure meant the recommendations were never of use.

braddock-self-confidence-fatal.text: Judged Braddock a brave man but fatally overconfident — too high an opinion of regular troops and too low an opinion of Americans and Indians; slighted George Croghan's hundred Indian scouts who then left him.

braddock-wagon-shortage.text: Braddock's expedition had only 25 wagons when 150 were necessary — the general declared the expedition impossible; Franklin undertook to procure wagons from Pennsylvania.

bradford-post-office-rivalry.text: Bradford used his post-office position to deny Franklin newspaper distribution; Franklin bribed post-riders to carry his papers and resolved never to use the same tactic when he later held the postmaster position.

bradford-referral-philadelphia.text: William Bradford referred Franklin to his son in Philadelphia, where a printer's hand had just died.

breintnal-junto-member.text: Joseph Breintnal — copier of deeds for scriveners, good-natured, middle-aged, lover of poetry, ingenious in nicknackeries, sensible conversation — was a founding Junto member.

british-regulars-myth-exploded.text: Braddock's defeat gave Americans the first suspicion that their exalted ideas of British regular troops' prowess were not well founded.

burlington-friends-acquired.text: During the Burlington paper-money job, acquired lasting friends among principal people of the province — Judge Allen, Bustill, Pearson, Cooper, Smiths, Decow — who continued their regard as long as they lived.

busy-body-series.text: Wrote the Busy Body series for Bradford's paper to divert public attention from Keimer's newspaper proposals; Breintnal continued the series for several months.

candid-about-own-errors.text: Acknowledges his own foolish disclosures and errata candidly rather than concealing them.

nudges.note: Called the Webb disclosure 'foolish'; wrote Vernon an ingenuous letter of acknowledgment for a debt long outstanding.

candid-about-vanity.text: Candid and self-aware about personal vanity, viewing it as sometimes productive rather than purely a vice.

nudges.note: Openly confessed to gratifying his own vanity in writing; argued vanity can produce good for oneself and others.
Acknowledged that early ballad sales flattered his vanity; notes when his victories in argument were undeserved.
Recognized that praise for anonymous essays flattered his vanity; admits James probably had reason to worry it made Franklin too vain.
Deliberately displayed silver and watch before James's journeymen — a vain show he later acknowledged offended his brother greatly.

cannon-borrowed-clinton.text: Borrowed eighteen eighteen-pound cannon from Governor Clinton of New York — won by degrees over a dinner of Madeira wine; the cannon were mounted on Philadelphia's new river battery.

carlisle-treaty-commissioner.text: Served as treaty commissioner at Carlisle with Speaker Norris — negotiated with Indians, forbade liquor during treaty, gave rum afterward; concluded to mutual satisfaction.

charleston-partnership-widow.text: Set up a Charleston printing partnership in 1733; the journeyman partner gave poor accounts but his Dutch widow kept exemplary accounts and eventually purchased the printing-house.

china-bowl-silver-spoon.text: First plate and china appeared in the house when Deborah secretly bought a China bowl and silver spoon for 23 shillings — afterward grew gradually to several hundred pounds in value as wealth increased.

city-paving-bill-1757.text: Drew a city paving bill and introduced it to the Assembly just before leaving for England in 1757; it passed after he left, with street-lighting added — a great improvement.

civic-indispensable.text: Regarded by peers as indispensable to any public-spirited project — no scheme moves without his involvement.

nudges.note: Bond explicitly told Franklin that subscribers would not commit until they knew Franklin approved — a standing recognition of his civic indispensability.

clerk-never-resign-rule.text: Adopted the rule of never asking for, refusing, or resigning an office — warned not to resign the Assembly clerkship, he refused; was unanimously re-elected.

coleman-grace-rescue.text: Coleman and Grace each independently offered to advance all the money needed to let Franklin take the printing business alone when the Meredith capital collapsed — two true friends whose kindness Franklin says he can never forget.

coleman-junto-member-lifelong-friend.text: William Coleman — merchant's clerk, coolest head, best heart, exactest morals — was a founding Junto member; his friendship with Franklin continued uninterrupted for over forty years until his death.

collins-debt-to-franklin.text: Collins borrowed heavily from Vernon's money Franklin was holding, promising to repay once employed but never did; he left for Barbados and was never heard from again.
