collins-fallen-drunkenness.text: Collins, once a sober and industrious lad with great mathematical genius and respected by clergy, fell into daily drunkenness and gambling during Franklin's absence from Boston.

colonelcy-declined.text: Accepted the colonelcy of the Philadelphia regiment on return from the frontier — twelve hundred men with an artillery company who could fire twelve rounds a minute.

history.value: Was chosen colonel by the Philadelphia regiment officers but declined, recommending Mr. Lawrence — judging himself unfit for that station.

commission-of-peace-alderman.text: After retiring from private business was appointed to the commission of the peace, chosen to the common council, and made an alderman — all unsolicited.

copley-medal-1753.text: Awarded the Copley Gold Medal of the Royal Society for 1753 — delivered by Governor Denny, accompanied by a handsome speech from Lord Macclesfield.

cunning-for-public-good.text: Willing to use strategic cunning in service of public benefit — and can excuse himself for it when the ends are beneficial.

nudges.note: Explicitly notes the hospital conditional clause was the political manoeuvre he most easily excused himself for using cunning — pride in the cleverness as well as the outcome.

cunning-hospital-maneuver.text: Regarded the conditional hospital bill as the political manoeuvre whose success gave him the most pleasure, and the one he most easily excused himself for making use of cunning.

david-hall-partnership.text: David Hall took over all care of the printing office as Franklin's partner from circa 1748 — paying Franklin his share punctually; the partnership lasted eighteen years.

deborah-first-sight.text: Married Deborah Read on 1 September 1730 — she proved a good and faithful helpmate, attended the shop, and they throve together and endeavored to make each other happy.

history.value: Deborah Read first saw Franklin on his ragged arrival in Philadelphia; he was walking up Market Street eating a roll and thought he made a most awkward, ridiculous appearance.

deborah-helpmate-shop.text: Deborah Franklin attended the printing shop and was a material help to the business.

deborah-london-erratum-corrected.text: Franklin regarded his giddiness and inconstancy in London as a great degree the cause of Deborah's unhappy first marriage; taking her to wife in 1730 was correcting that great erratum as well as he could.

deborah-married-rogers.text: While Franklin was in London, Deborah Read was persuaded to marry Rogers the potter — an unhappy union; she soon separated from him, and Rogers died in the West Indies.

deborah-neglected-london.text: Wrote only one letter to Deborah Read from London — saying he was unlikely to return soon — and gradually let his engagements to her lapse; he called this another great erratum.

deborah-read-courtship-pre-england.text: Made some courtship to Deborah Read before sailing for England; her mother thought it prudent to wait for his return and establishment in business.

defense-commissioner-60k.text: Appointed one of the commissioners for disposing of sixty thousand pounds voted by the Assembly for defense — having been active in modelling the bill and procuring its passage.

denham-clerk-offer.text: Denham hired Franklin as his clerk at 50 pounds a year Pennsylvania money to manage his Philadelphia store.

denham-debt-repayment-bristol.text: Denham had formerly failed in debt at Bristol, compounded with creditors, went to America, made a fortune, then surprised every old creditor at a dinner by placing a full repayment order under each plate — a trait of character Franklin recorded with admiration.

denham-died-legacy.text: Denham died of his illness early 1727, leaving Franklin a small legacy in a nuncupative will as a token of his kindness.

denham-friendship-voyage.text: Mr. Denham contracted a friendship for Franklin on the England voyage that continued during his life.

denny-bribe-rebuffed.text: Rebuffed Governor Denny's private offer of implied rewards for moderating Assembly opposition — told him that his circumstances made proprietary favours unnecessary and that his opposition had always been grounded in the public good.

denny-turned-out.text: The proprietaries turned out Governor Denny and threatened to sue him for breach of instructions — but Denny had powerful court interests and the threats were never executed.

diffident-habit-civic-influence.text: Attributes his early weight with fellow-citizens when proposing new institutions to the habit of diffident expression — not to eloquence, in which he was deficient.

disliked-tallow-trade.text: Disliked his father's tallow-chandler trade and had a strong inclination for the sea as a boy.

disputes-hurt-good-will.text: Believes disputing, contradicting, and confuting people get victory but not good will — and good will is of more use than victory in affairs.

nudges.note: Observed of Governor Morris: eloquent sophister, loved disputing, was generally successful in argument, but fell into ruinous contention with the Assembly — confirming Franklin's long-held view.

dunbar-broke-promise-servants.text: Colonel Dunbar, on command after Braddock's death, refused to discharge three Lancaster farmers' enlisted servants despite promising to do so at Trenton — a broken promise causing loss and disappointment.

dunkers-no-fixed-creed.text: Heard from Dunker founder Michael Welfare that their sect refused to publish a confession of faith lest they be bound by it and prevented from further spiritual improvement — Franklin admired this unusual modesty.

early-leader-boys.text: Was generally a leader among boyhood companions, commonly allowed to govern in boats and in any case of difficulty.

early-reading-books.text: From childhood was fond of reading and spent all spare money on books; began with Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, then Burton's Historical Collections.

effacement-as-tactic.text: Learned to put himself out of sight when proposing public projects — attributing proposals to 'a number of friends' to avoid provoking envy; the sacrifice of vanity is repaid when rivals' false claims restore the credit to its rightful owner.

electrical-papers-published.text: Franklin's electrical letters to Collinson were read at the Royal Society but initially laughed at; Fothergill rescued them for publication — first in Gentleman's Magazine, then as a quarto volume that went through five editions at no cost to Cave.

electricity-europe-adopted.text: Franklin's electrical doctrine was universally adopted by European philosophers — the book translated into Italian, German, and Latin; Nollet ended as the last of his sect.

employed-men-content.text: Observed that employed men are best contented — on work days the troops were good-natured and cheerful; idle days brought mutiny and quarreling.

explicit-articles-prevent-quarrels.text: Recommends that all business partnerships have every obligation and expectation explicitly written into articles — reduces jealousies and ends amicably.

nudges.note: All his printing partnerships ended amicably; attributes this to explicit articles settling everything in advance.

family-religion-nonconformist.text: Family was Protestant through the reign of Queen Mary; Josiah and uncle Benjamin became Nonconformists at the end of Charles II's reign.

family-roots-ecton.text: Family lived in Ecton, Northamptonshire for at least three hundred years on a freehold of about thirty acres, practicing the smith's trade.

father-josiah-children.text: Josiah Franklin had seventeen children in total — seven by his first wife and ten by his second wife Abiah.

fire-company-founded.text: Founded a fire company with thirty associates — each kept leather buckets, bags, and baskets; the company met monthly and was much imitated across Philadelphia.

fort-gnadenhut-built.text: Built a palisade fort at Gnadenhut in one week — four hundred fifty-five foot circumference, completed despite alternate-day rain; three forts total built on the frontier.

fothergill-street-sweeping.text: Proposed a dry-weather street-sweeping system to Dr. Fothergill in London — sweeping before rain fell would prevent the deeper mud problem.

frontier-commission.text: Received a full commission from the governor to raise troops and build forts on the north-western frontier — commanded five hundred sixty men with son William as aide-de-camp.

frs-elected.text: Elected a Fellow of the Royal Society without application — fees of twenty-five guineas excused; thereafter received the Transactions gratis.

frugal-public-image.text: Deliberately manages public image of industry and frugality as a business asset.

nudges.note: Dressed plainly, avoided diversions, and carried paper on a wheelbarrow to show he was not above his business — and it worked: merchants solicited his custom.

frugality-reputation-strategy.text: Deliberately cultivated the appearance of frugality — dressed plainly, avoided idle diversions, carried paper home on a wheelbarrow — to secure credit and tradesman character while paying off printing-house debts.

generous-when-little.text: Observed himself more generous when he had little money than when he had plenty — perhaps from fear of being thought poor.

godfrey-courtship-broken.text: Mrs. Godfrey arranged a courtship with a relation's daughter that ended when the family, advised by Bradford that the printing business was failing, forbade the house and shut up the daughter.

godfrey-junto-member.text: Thomas Godfrey — self-taught mathematician, later inventor of Hadley's Quadrant — was a Junto member; expected universal precision, was not a pleasing companion, and soon left.

governor-burnet-visit.text: Governor Burnet of New York (son of Bishop Burnet) invited Franklin to see him on hearing he carried many books; showed his large library and conversed about books and authors.

grandfather-thomas-1598.text: Paternal grandfather Thomas Franklin was born in 1598 and died at Banbury while living with his son John.

granville-king-legislator-doctrine.text: Lord Granville asserted that the king is the sole legislator of the colonies and his instructions to governors are laws — a doctrine Franklin found new, alarming, and contrary to his understanding of colonial charters.

gratitude-prompts-generosity.text: Grateful for early kindnesses; gratitude later makes him more ready to help young beginners

nudges.note: The first five-shilling customer's gratitude — 'has made me often more ready than perhaps I should otherwise have been to assist young beginners.'

great-uncle-thomas-scrivener.text: Great-uncle Thomas Franklin trained as a smith but became a notable scrivener and public-spirited leader in Northamptonshire, dying 6 January 1702.

hamilton-assembly-patronage.text: Andrew Hamilton returned from England with a seat in the Assembly and strongly interceded for Franklin in the printer appointment, as he did in many instances afterward until his death.

hamilton-friend-through-riddlesden.text: Warned Andrew Hamilton about Riddlesden's letter and the scheme against him; Hamilton became Franklin's friend, greatly to his advantage on many later occasions.

heeds-wise-counsel.text: Heeds wise counsel from others even when initially skeptical

nudges.note: Heeded the Quaker matron's warning about the two women despite initial doubt, which saved him from trouble.
Was inclined to travel Europe with Wygate but Denham dissuaded him toward returning to Pennsylvania — he followed the advice.

hemphill-championed-quitted-congregation.text: Championed Hemphill against the Presbyterian synod, writing pamphlets in his defence; after defeat and discovery of plagiarism, quitted the congregation — though continued subscription support for its ministers for many years.

holmes-introduced-to-keith.text: Captain Holmes showed Franklin's letter to Governor Keith, which prompted Keith's interest in Franklin and his patronage offer.

honesty-over-clever-ends.text: Holds that nothing useful can be dishonest — ends do not justify dishonest means.

nudges.note: Father convinced him during the wharf-stone episode that nothing is useful which is not honest.
Acknowledged exploiting secret indentures to gain freedom as 'not fair' — calls it one of the first errata of his life.

honorary-degrees.text: Received honorary Master of Arts degrees from Yale and from Harvard (College of Cambridge) without study — conferred in recognition of electrical discoveries.

hospital-championed-1751.text: Dr. Thomas Bond conceived the Pennsylvania Hospital in 1751 — Franklin subscribed and secured further subscriptions after preparing public opinion through newspaper writing.

hospital-conditional-bill.text: Devised a conditional clause: the Assembly would grant 2,000 pounds only once private subscriptions reached the required capital — the clause worked both ways to attract both votes and donors.

human-felicity-small-things.text: Holds that human felicity is produced more by small daily advantages than by great pieces of good fortune — justifies attention to seemingly low civic matters.

indifference-to-food.text: Raised with such inattention to food that he remained largely indifferent to what was set before him throughout his life — a practical advantage when travelling.

indifferent-to-food-comfort.text: Indifferent to food and culinary comfort, finding it a practical advantage.

nudges.note: Could rarely recall hours later what he had eaten — traced directly to father's dinner-table habits.

industrious-self-disciplined.text: Works with exceptional, visible industry — stays at the press later and rises earlier than anyone around him.

nudges.note: Reset broken form pages past eleven at night rather than leave the work; Dr. Baird remarked his industry was superior to any he had ever seen.

industry-visible-reputation.text: Franklin's industry was visible to neighbors — Dr. Baird noted he was still at work when Baird went home from club and was at work again before neighbors were out of bed; this gave the shop character and credit.

inventions-freely-given.text: Holds that inventions should be shared freely and generously, not patented for personal profit — we owe a debt to those whose inventions we enjoy.

nudges.note: Declined patent for Pennsylvania Fireplace on explicit principle; never contested others who patented his ideas.

james-franklin-reconciled-deathbed.text: Visited James in Newport after ten years — former differences forgotten; James, near death, asked Franklin to raise his ten-year-old son in the printing trade, which Franklin did.

james-violent-master.text: James frequently beat Franklin in passion — behavior Franklin resented deeply, though he acknowledged James was not otherwise ill-natured.

john-franklin-newport.text: Brother John was married and settled in Newport, Rhode Island.

josiah-advice-return-philadelphia.text: Josiah counseled steady industry and prudent parsimony, avoidance of lampooning, and promised to help Franklin set up once he turned twenty-one.

josiah-character.text: Josiah had a sound understanding and solid judgment in public and private affairs; frequently consulted by town leaders and chosen as arbitrator.

josiah-death-age.text: Josiah Franklin died at age 89, born 1655.

josiah-refused-keith-plan.text: Josiah declined Governor Keith's plan as premature — Franklin was three years short of legal majority and too young to manage so important a business.

josiah-solomon-proverb.text: Father frequently repeated Solomon's proverb: 'Seest thou a man diligent in his calling, he shall stand before kings' — Franklin took it to heart as encouragement for industry; he later literally stood before five kings.

josiah-table-habits.text: Josiah habitually invited a sensible friend or neighbor to dinner to converse on improving topics, paying little attention to the food itself.

josiah-trade-tallow-chandler.text: Josiah Franklin's trade in Boston was tallow-chandler and soap-boiler, which he took up on finding his dyeing trade would not support his family.

junto-best-school.text: The Junto was the best school of philosophy, morality, and politics that then existed in the province; the club continued almost as long as Franklin's friendship with Coleman — over forty years.

junto-book-pool.text: Proposed pooling Junto members' books in a shared room at Grace's house — the experiment worked for about a year but ended from careless handling.

junto-founded.text: Founded the Junto in the autumn before the printing-house opened — a Friday-evening club of mutual improvement, rules drafted by Franklin, debating morals, politics, and natural philosophy.

junto-rules-positiveness-banned.text: Junto rules required members to produce queries and essays, and after some time made all positiveness in opinions and direct contradiction contraband under small pecuniary penalties.

junto-subordinate-clubs.text: Proposed and created five or six subordinate clubs (Vine, Union, Band, etc.) connected to the Junto but kept secret from their members — used to extend Junto influence on public opinion.

keimer-employer-philadelphia.text: Keimer agreed to employ Franklin in Philadelphia; Franklin judged him a mere novice easily duped by Bradford's craft.

keimer-factotum.text: At Keimer's second stint served as complete factotum — cast types from contrived mould, made ink, engraved, and managed warehouse; services became less important as other hands improved.

keimer-paper-acquired.text: Keimer ran his newspaper for three-quarters of a year with at most ninety subscribers, then sold it to Franklin for a trifle; it proved extremely profitable within a few years.

keimer-sect-proposal.text: Keimer proposed that Franklin be his colleague in founding a new religious sect — Keimer to preach, Franklin to confound opponents.

keimer-vegetarian-scheme.text: Maneuvered Keimer into a three-month vegetarian diet as part of religious sect negotiations; the whim also suited Franklin for the cheapness — about eighteenpence each per week.

keimer-walked-out.text: Walked out of Keimer's printing-house after a public rebuke from the street — Keimer had grown increasingly difficult as Franklin's indispensability faded.

keith-liberal-promises.text: Governor Keith kept deferring the promised letters of recommendation and credit for England; at Newcastle the secretary came with polite excuses — the letters were never actually delivered.

history.value: Keith was later known to be liberal of promises he never meant to keep — Franklin was unaware of this at the time and believed him one of the best men in the world.

keith-no-letters-confirmed.text: Confirmed in London that Governor Keith had sent no letters at all — the bag contained only a Riddlesden letter; Keith had no credit to give and was known to all as unreliable.

keith-no-longer-governor.text: On return to Philadelphia in 1726 found Keith had been superseded as governor by Major Gordon and was walking the streets as a common citizen.

keith-patronage-offer.text: Governor Keith offered to procure public printing business for Franklin and to write Josiah a letter endorsing the plan to set him up in Philadelphia.

key-books-essay-on-projects.text: Defoe's Essay on Projects and Dr. Mather's Essays to do Good influenced his thinking and shaped principal future events of his life.

kite-experiment.text: Performed the kite experiment at Philadelphia — drawing lightning from clouds and confirming the sameness of lightning with electricity.

lamp-design-improvement.text: Improved Philadelphia street-lamp design — four flat panes with a top funnel and bottom air crevices kept lamps bright all night, unlike London's globe lamps that darkened within hours.

language-study-1733.text: Beginning in 1733 mastered French, Italian, and Spanish by reading; learned Italian through chess-game language tasks with an acquaintance; found these three languages later smoothed recovery of Latin.

left-boston-age-17.text: Left Boston secretly at age seventeen, arriving in New York nearly 300 miles from home with very little money.

lets-work-speak.text: Lets verifiable work speak for itself rather than entering public disputes — prefers making new experiments to defending old ones.

nudges.note: Declined to answer Nollet's volume of attacks — reasoned that experiments which could be verified needed no defence, and that time was better spent on new work.

liberty-necessity-pamphlet.text: Wrote 'A Dissertation on Liberty and Necessity, Pleasure and Pain' at Palmer's — considered it another erratum; it impressed Palmer but he found its principles abominable.

library-self-study.text: Used the library for an hour or two of study each day, repairing the loss of the learned education his father had intended for him.

lightning-sameness-paper.text: Wrote a paper for Kinnersley on the sameness of lightning with electricity — sent to Dr. Mitchel at the Royal Society; it was read but laughed at by the connoisseurs.

loan-office-orders-crown-point.text: Proposed interest-bearing Loan Office orders payable in a year to fund Crown Point aid when the governor blocked a regular bill — the orders were eagerly bought up and the business completed.

lodgings-duke-street.text: Moved to lodgings in Duke Street, opposite the Romish Chapel, at 1s 6d per week — landlady reduced rent from 3s 6d in exchange for his company and protection.

london-agency-success.text: The London agency succeeded in its primary goal — the proprietary tax act was preserved and the paper money currency secured; the autobiography ends at this point, unfinished.

london-total-stay.text: Spent about eighteen months total in London; Ralph owed him about 27 pounds never likely to be recovered.

loudoun-accused-franklin-pocketing.text: Loudoun accused Franklin of pocketing money from army provisioning — refused to believe Franklin had not profited; Franklin denied it and was offended by the insinuation.

loudoun-campaign-disgraceful.text: Loudoun's 1757 campaign was frivolous, expensive, and disgraceful — left the colonies exposed while parading at Halifax; Fort George was lost; he derailed trade with a long embargo and returned the troops without any action.

loudoun-indecision.text: Lord Loudoun's defining flaw was indecision — detained four packet-boats and hundreds of passengers for months with letters always promised for tomorrow; Pitt later cited this as his reason for replacing Loudoun with Amherst and Wolfe.

loyalty-before-interest.text: Holds obligations to those who helped him above his own immediate interest — delays accepting better offers rather than abandon a partner while there is prospect of that partner fulfilling his agreement.

nudges.note: Declined Coleman's and Grace's rescue offers so long as there was any prospect of the Merediths fulfilling their agreement, from a sense of obligation.

matthew-adams-books.text: Matthew Adams, a tradesman who frequented the printing-house, invited him to his library and kindly lent him books.

maugridge-grace-junto-members.text: William Maugridge (joiner, exquisite mechanic, solid and sensible) and Robert Grace (young gentleman of fortune, generous, lively, witty, lover of punning) were Junto members.

meetinghouse-any-preacher-built.text: A meetinghouse one hundred feet by seventy was built in Philadelphia for any preacher of any persuasion — including hypothetically a Mohammedan missionary — its ground and building vested in trustees for the general use of all inhabitants.

meredith-partnership-formed.text: The Meredith partnership was dissolved circa 1729 — Franklin took all debts, repaid the father's 100 pounds, paid personal debts, and gave Meredith 30 pounds and a new saddle; Meredith went to North Carolina.

history.value: Formed a printing partnership with Hugh Meredith — Meredith's father to furnish capital for press and types; Franklin's skill the other stake; profits to be shared equally.

meredith-poor-partner.text: Meredith was no compositor, a poor pressman, and seldom sober; friends lamented the connection, but Franklin made the best of it.

mickle-croaker-visit.text: Samuel Mickle stopped at Franklin's printing-house door to predict the city's ruin and the venture's failure; Franklin was left half-melancholy but later saw Mickle pay five times the price for a house he had refused to buy.

militia-bill-passed.text: Drew and passed a voluntary militia bill through the Assembly, carefully leaving Quakers at liberty — also wrote a dialogue on militia objections that had great effect.

militia-commissions-broken.text: All militia commissions were broken when England repealed the militia law — Franklin's colonelcy was short-lived.

modest-diffidence-habit.text: Habitually expresses opinions with modest diffidence rather than positive assertion.

nudges.note: Consciously replaced disputatious contradiction with 'I conceive' / 'it appears to me' — practiced lifelong.

modest-diffidence-speech.text: Adopted a lifelong habit of modest diffidence in expression — never using 'certainly' or 'undoubtedly', preferring 'I conceive', 'it appears to me', 'I should think'.

moral-perfection-project-conceived.text: Conceived the bold and arduous project of arriving at moral perfection — living without committing any fault — and quickly found the task harder than imagined, concluding that good habits must be built to make virtue steady.

moravian-surprise-defense.text: Found the Moravian community at Bethlehem surprisingly well prepared — stockades, New York arms, paving stones for women to throw; Bishop Spangenberg noted their pacifism was not a firm principle.

morris-disputer-no-personal-rift.text: Governor Morris was an eloquent, acute sophister who loved disputing — despite constant public quarrel with the Assembly, no personal difference arose between him and Franklin; they often dined together.

morris-no-personal-rift.text: Despite constant public quarrel between Governor Morris and the Assembly, maintained a civil personal intercourse — Morris sometimes consulted Franklin privately and occasionally took his advice.

mother-abiah-lineage.text: Mother Abiah Folger was the daughter of Peter Folger, a godly, learned Englishman and one of the first settlers of New England.

moved-by-eloquence-despite-resolve.text: Can be moved by excellent oratory to act against prior resolve — susceptible to rhetorical persuasion even when consciously guarded.

nudges.note: Resolved not to give to Whitefield's collection then emptied his entire pocket — gold and all — by the end of the sermon.

near-shipwreck-falmouth.text: Nearly wrecked on rocks near Falmouth approaching England — the lighthouse appeared as big as a cart-wheel before Captain Kennedy ordered the ship to wear round; resolved to encourage building more lighthouses in America.

new-england-courant.text: James Franklin's New England Courant, begun around 1720-1721, was the second newspaper in America; Franklin managed it and wrote anonymous essays for it.

new-jersey-copperplate-press.text: Designed and built the first copperplate press seen in the colonies for the New Jersey paper-money job; executed the full job at Burlington.

newcastle-printing-contract.text: Hamilton obtained for Franklin the Newcastle paper-money printing contract and the ongoing contract to print that government's laws and votes.

newspaper-no-libel-policy.text: Ran the Gazette refusing all libelling and personal abuse — would print scandalous pieces separately but not spread detraction through subscriber papers; urged this as a model for young printers.

nollet-not-answered.text: Decided not to answer Abbé Nollet's published attacks — reasoning that experiments that could be verified needed no defense, and that new experiments were more valuable than old disputes.

officers-parcels-sent.text: Arranged 20 parcels of camp necessaries for Dunbar's regiment subalterns — wrote to the Assembly committee on their behalf; the officers acknowledged the kindness in grateful letters.

one-man-great-changes.text: Believes one person of tolerable abilities, with a good plan and undivided attention, can work great changes among mankind.

nudges.note: Stated explicitly when reflecting on the United Party for Virtue — never discouraged by magnitude of an undertaking.

order-weak-spot.text: Has a lifelong weak spot for orderliness — papers, places for things, scheduling; incorrigible despite the most painful attention.

nudges.note: Found Order the most troublesome virtue — never successfully acquired the habit; relied on good memory instead; felt the want of it acutely in old age.

osborne-pact-after-death.text: Osborne and Franklin made a serious agreement that whichever died first would, if possible, visit the other and report on the afterlife — Osborne died first and never fulfilled the promise.

others-patented-his-inventions.text: An London ironmonger patented a modified version of the Pennsylvania Fireplace and made a small fortune — not the only case of others taking patents for Franklin's inventions, which he never contested.

own-shop-opened.text: Opened own printing shop near the Philadelphia market with Meredith; first customer brought by George House paid five shillings — more pleasurable than any crown since earned.

palmer-printing-london.text: Got work immediately at Palmer's printing-house in Bartholomew Close, London; stayed nearly a year.

paper-currency-pamphlet.text: Wrote and printed 'The Nature and Necessity of a Paper Currency' anonymously — it swayed public and Assembly opinion, defeated wealthy opposition, and won him the profitable contract to print the new money.

parents-marriage-length.text: Josiah and Abiah Franklin lived lovingly together in wedlock fifty-five years.

patent-refused-on-principle.text: Declined Governor Thomas's patent for the Pennsylvania Fireplace on the principle that inventors should freely serve others with their inventions, as they themselves enjoy advantages from others' inventions.

pennsylvania-fireplace-invented.text: Invented the Pennsylvania Fireplace (open stove) in 1742 — gave the model freely to Robert Grace; wrote a promoting pamphlet; declined a governor's patent; an London ironmonger later patented a version and made a fortune.

philadelphia-street-paving.text: Got a section of Philadelphia market street paved with stone and organized a neighborhood sweeping scheme at sixpence per month — the success bred a general city desire for paving.

philosophical-society-founded-1744.text: Proposed and established the American Philosophical Society in 1744.

plain-truth-pamphlet.text: Wrote and published Plain Truth — a pamphlet on Pennsylvania's defenceless situation — which swiftly gathered over twelve hundred Philadelphia signatures and ten thousand province-wide for a voluntary defense association.

pleurisy-near-death.text: Fell ill with pleurisy in early February 1726-7, just past his twenty-first year; nearly died but recovered.

poor-richard-annual-sales.text: Poor Richard's Almanac sold nearly ten thousand copies annually — one of the most widely read publications in the province, reaching neighborhoods that bought scarcely any other books.

poor-richard-proverbs-purpose.text: Filled the almanac's calendar spaces with proverbs chiefly inculcating industry and frugality — using it as a vehicle to convey instruction to common people who bought few other books.

post-office-turned-profitable.text: After four years in debt, the American post office was brought to yield three times the revenue of the Irish post office to the crown — until Franklin was displaced by a ministerial freak.

postmaster-appointed-1737.text: Appointed joint Postmaster General of America with William Hunter in 1753 on the death of the previous holder — salary of 600 pounds to be split if they could earn it from profits.

history.value: Appointed Philadelphia deputy postmaster-general by Colonel Spotswood in 1737 — salary small but greatly facilitated newspaper correspondence and boosted income; Bradford's paper declined as a result.

practical-over-ideological.text: Chooses practical prudence over rigid principle when the principle creates needless conflict

nudges.note: Paid the bien venu compositors' fee after weeks of resistance, concluding it was folly to be on ill terms with those one lives with continually.

practical-problem-solver.text: Solves human problems with practical incentive design rather than punishment or preaching.

nudges.note: The Beatty rum-prayer solution — instead of punishment for non-attendance, used the rum ration as a motivating reward after prayers.

pride-incorrigible-admitted.text: Admits pride is the hardest passion to subdue — it persists and peeps out; even believing oneself rid of it would be a form of pride.

private-liturgy-1728.text: Composed a private liturgy, titled 'Articles of Belief and Acts of Religion,' for his own use in 1728; returned to it after abandoning public worship.

proprietary-talks-stalled.text: Talks with Penn proprietaries at Spring Garden stalled — Franklin submitted written complaints but they were handed to Paris and to the Attorney and Solicitor-General, where they lay unanswered for nearly a year; proprietaries finally sent a flimsy message impugning Franklin's candour.

proprietary-tax-act-passed.text: The Pennsylvania tax act on the proprietary estate was allowed to pass — thanks to a private compromise brokered by Lord Mansfield; Franklin gave his personal assurance the estate would not be unfairly assessed.

proprietary-tax-exemption-quarrel.text: The proprietary governors were instructed not to pass tax acts unless their vast estates were exempted — causing three years of Assembly resistance; the source of the public quarrels of the Morris era.

proprietor-rancour.text: The proprietor's rancour against Franklin grew — stoked by the officer-escort incident and Franklin's Assembly opposition to exempting the proprietary estate from taxation; proprietor accused him to the ministry and tried to have him removed as postmaster.

prose-writing-key-skill.text: Prose writing was a principal means of advancement throughout his life.

providential-gratitude.text: Attributes personal success to divine providence and maintains humble gratitude toward God.

nudges.note: Explicitly acknowledged that his happiness was owed to God's kind providence, not solely his own efforts.

prudently-remove-not-resent.text: Removes opposition prudently rather than retaliating — sees revenge as less profitable than a well-timed conciliatory gesture.

nudges.note: Turned Assembly adversary to friend via book borrowing; noted satisfaction when Bradford suffered from his own neglect without Franklin retaliating.

public-opinion-newspaper-prep.text: Habitually prepared public minds through newspaper writing before soliciting subscriptions or support for civic projects — his usual custom.

public-spirited-first-mover.text: Takes initiative to create public institutions and shared goods — and learned to suppress his own visible role to avoid envy.

nudges.note: Noted family tradition of public-spiritedness in great-uncle Thomas; saw his own rise as a model worth sharing with posterity.
Built wharf for public use as a child; even when ethically misguided (stealing stones), the impulse was to improve shared conditions.
Gave away two rolls to a woman and child in need, keeping only one for himself despite having almost no money.
The subscription library was explicitly called his 'first project of a public nature' — proposed and organized the whole himself.
Explicitly states the lesson: put yourself out of sight when proposing public projects — the present sacrifice of vanity is repaid.

quaker-defense-minority-small.text: Estimated that only one in twenty-one Quakers was sincerely against defense — the majority either voted for the battery lottery or absented themselves rather than oppose it.

ralph-debt-lost-friendship.text: After Franklin attempted familiarities with Mrs. T, Ralph declared all his debts to Franklin cancelled and the friendship ended; Franklin concluded he would never be repaid but felt relieved of a burden.

ralph-prosperous-england.text: Learned from Governor Denny that James Ralph was alive and prosperous in England — esteemed one of the best political writers, earned a pension of 300 pounds a year, though Pope had damned his poetry in the Dunciad.

ralph-unsettled-religion.text: Ralph, like Collins, had his religious principles unsettled by Franklin — for which both later made Franklin suffer.

ralph-wife-abandoned.text: Ralph accompanied Franklin to England despite being married with one child; his true intent was to abandon his wife's relations and never return.

rationalizes-desire.text: Finds reasons to justify what he already wants to do — a candid self-aware rationalizer

nudges.note: Broke vegetarian principle by reasoning that fish eat each other, then observed: 'So convenient a thing it is to be a reasonable creature.'
Adopted a three-month vegetarian diet with Keimer partly for the cheapness — a practical motive alongside the philosophical one.
Attempted familiarities with Mrs. T 'being at that time under no religious restraint' — his own candid framing.

read-locke-navigation.text: Read Locke's On Human Understanding, Seller's and Shermy's Navigation books, and du Port Royal's Art of Thinking in his teens.

religious-creed-five-essentials.text: Settled on five essentials held to be common to all religions: existence of the Deity, Providence, doing good to man as best service to God, immortality of the soul, and that virtue and crime are rewarded and punished.

religious-position-deist.text: Became a thorough Deist at about fifteen after anti-Deist books had the opposite of their intended effect; later concluded that while Deism might be true, it was not very useful, and formed written resolutions of truth, sincerity, and integrity.

religious-skeptic-reputation.text: Indiscreet religious disputations in Boston made him regarded by good people as an infidel or atheist.

resumed-writing-home-1788.text: Resumed writing the autobiography at home in August 1788, unable to use expected papers as many were lost in the war.

returned-philadelphia-1726.text: Landed in Philadelphia on 11 October 1726, after sailing from Gravesend 23 July 1726.

rise-from-obscurity.text: Rose from poverty and obscurity to a state of affluence and some degree of reputation in the world.

school-grammar-quick-rise.text: At grammar school rose quickly from mid-class to head of class within a year before being withdrawn.

scull-parsons-junto-members.text: Nicholas Scull (surveyor, later surveyor-general, loved books) and William Parsons (shoemaker turned mathematician, later surveyor-general) were Junto members.

sea-plan-future-conduct.text: Formed a plan at sea on the return voyage for regulating his future conduct in life — remarkable for being formed so young and faithfully adhered to into old age.

second-governor-notice.text: Governor Burnet was the second governor to honor Franklin with personal notice — very pleasing to a poor boy.

secret-indenture-scheme.text: After Assembly banned James from printing the Courant, old indentures were returned to Franklin and secret new ones signed — a flimsy scheme Franklin later called his first erratum.

self-improvement-systematic.text: Approaches self-improvement methodically and systematically, constructing deliberate exercises.

nudges.note: Designed an elaborate self-teaching regime with the Spectator — reducing, rewriting, jumbling, re-ordering — to build prose style and method.
Even on the journey to Philadelphia, treated fever with a rational remedy read somewhere; pressed on resolutely despite exhaustion.
Gained money through industry and frugality in Philadelphia; Josiah praised his industriousness in equipping himself so handsomely in so short a time.
Mastered French, Italian, Spanish, and recovered Latin entirely through reading and self-imposed exercises — no teachers mentioned.

self-reflection-writing.text: Inclined to reflect on life experience and commit it to durable written form.

nudges.note: Deliberately began writing autobiography to make recollection of his life as durable as possible.
Acknowledges growing old by his digressive style; remarks that one does not dress for private company as for a public ball.

ship-trim-observation.text: Observed and noted that a ship's sailing quality depends on systematic loading and rigging — proposed that a set of accurate experiments could determine the best hull, mast, sail, and lading design, expressing the scientific method he applied to all problems.

shirley-capable-commander.text: Franklin regarded General Shirley as a sensible, sagacious commander who would have made a far better campaign than Loudoun — attentive to good advice and quick to execute judicious plans.

sloane-asbestos-purse.text: Sold an asbestos purse curiosity to Sir Hans Sloane, who paid handsomely for it.

society-free-and-easy-planned.text: Planned the Society of the Free and Easy — a secret society of virtuous young men practicing the thirteen-virtue regimen, pledged to mutual support, free from vice and debt.

socratic-method-adopted-then-moderated.text: Practiced the Socratic method for some years — artfully drawing opponents into concessions — then abandoned its combative form while keeping modest diffidence.

socratic-method-keimer.text: Used the Socratic method so effectively on Keimer that Keimer grew ridiculously cautious and would not answer even common questions without asking what Franklin intended to infer.

son-appointed-assembly-clerk.text: On Franklin taking his seat in the Assembly, his son was appointed clerk of the House.

son-died-smallpox-1736.text: Lost a four-year-old son to smallpox in 1736 — regretted bitterly not inoculating him, and regarded the regret as the same either way; urged inoculation on other parents.

spectator-self-study.text: Used the Spectator as a self-teaching model — converted essays to hints, rewrote them, compared with original, to develop style and method.

spence-apparatus-electrical.text: Purchased Dr. Spence's full electrical apparatus and began electrical experiments with great alacrity after retiring from private business.

subscription-library-founded.text: Founded the first public subscription library — fifty subscribers, 40 shillings each plus 10 shillings a year; later chartered and expanded to one hundred; the mother of all North American subscription libraries.

sunday-study-day.text: Kept Sunday as a day of study rather than public worship — having need of the leisure for his course of self-education.

swam-managed-boats.text: Learned early to swim well and to manage boats, growing up near the water in Boston.

swimming-chelsea-blackfriars.text: Swam from near Chelsea to Blackfriars in the Thames, performing feats from Thevenot's motions and his own additions, to the admiration of the company.

systematic-self-improver-virtue.text: Approaches ethical self-improvement with the same systematic, methodical spirit as intellectual self-improvement.

nudges.note: Devised thirteen precisely named virtues with precepts, and a method to work through them — treating character building as a project to be designed.
Designed a thirteen-week tracking system with a ruled book, daily examination questions, and a full daily schedule — treating virtue as a project to be engineered and measured.

tennent-fundraising-advice.text: Advised Tennent to ask everyone for subscriptions — first those who will give, then the uncertain, then even those sure to refuse — because some of the last would surprise him.

thirteen-virtues.text: Devised thirteen named virtues — Temperance, Silence, Order, Resolution, Frugality, Industry, Sincerity, Justice, Moderation, Cleanliness, Tranquillity, Chastity, Humility — each with a short precept.

uncle-benjamin-named-after.text: Named Benjamin after uncle Benjamin Franklin, owing to a particular affection between uncle Benjamin and Josiah.

uncle-benjamin-pamphlets.text: Uncle Benjamin assembled a collection of principal political pamphlets from 1641 to 1717, later found by Franklin in London.

united-party-never-executed.text: The United Party for Virtue was never prosecuted beyond sharing with two enthusiastic young men — narrow circumstances and multiplying public occupations caused indefinite postponement.

university-of-philadelphia.text: The academy was incorporated by the governor and grew into the University of Philadelphia — Franklin continued as trustee from the beginning for nearly forty years.

unsolicited-office.text: Receives public offices and honors without solicitation — pleased by them as spontaneous testimonies of public esteem.

nudges.note: Elected to Assembly, appointed alderman, justice of peace, common council — all unsolicited; admits ambition was flattered.

vaughan-letter.text: Benjamin Vaughan wrote from Paris (31 January 1783) urging Franklin to publish his autobiography as a guide to self-education and private character formation for future generations.

vegetable-diet-tryon.text: Broke his vegetarian resolve when becalmed off Block Island — ate cod and thereafter ate as others did, only occasionally returning to vegetables.

history.value: Adopted a vegetarian diet at age sixteen following Tryon's book; found it gave clearer head and quicker apprehension.

vernon-money-entrusted.text: Vernon entrusted Franklin with collecting about 35 pounds currency owed him in Pennsylvania and holding it until directed how to remit it.

vernon-money-erratum.text: Franklin repaid Vernon the principal with interest, and was thanked for his honest acknowledgment; the Vernon erratum was in some degree corrected.

history.value: Breaking into Vernon's money was one of the first great errata of his life — he used it to support Collins and lived in daily apprehension of being called to repay it.

virtue-as-rational-self-interest.text: Frames virtue as rational self-interest rather than divine command — dishonesty is impractical, not merely forbidden.

nudges.note: The Art of Virtue doctrine: vicious acts are hurtful first, forbidden second; virtue is every person's worldly interest.

virtue-book-carried-always.text: Always carried the little virtue-examination book with him even after the formal courses were abandoned.

virtue-daily-schedule.text: Created a daily schedule for the twenty-four hours — rising at 5, morning question 'What good shall I do today?', work blocks, noon reading and accounts, evening 'What good have I done?', examination, sleep by 1am.

virtue-project-order-incorrigible.text: Found Order the most troublesome of the thirteen virtues — incorrigible with respect to it, plagued by frequent relapses; never acquired the habit early and relied on a good memory instead; felt the want of it keenly in old age.

virtue-project-outcome.text: Never arrived at the perfection he aimed for but was, by the endeavor, a better and happier man than he otherwise would have been — as aiming at perfect writing improves the hand even without reaching the ideal copy.

virtue-project-outcomes-attributed.text: Ascribes his long health to Temperance, his early fortune to Industry and Frugality, the country's confidence to Sincerity and Justice, and his cheerful company to the mass of virtues — down to his 79th year.

virtue-pythagoras-addison-cicero.text: The virtue book bore mottos from Addison's Cato, Cicero on philosophy, and Proverbs of Solomon; prefixed a daily prayer to the Powerful Goodness asking for wisdom, strengthened resolutions, and acceptance of kind offices.

war-uncertainty.text: Maintains sober caution about military outcomes — refuses premature celebration because the events of war are subject to great uncertainty.

nudges.note: Discouraged the Bond brothers' firework subscription before Braddock's return; had foreseen the ambush risk; was proved right in both cases.

water-american-watts.text: At Watts's printing-house was nicknamed 'the Water-American' — drank only water while fifty workmen guzzled beer, and proved stronger than they were.

watts-chapel-bien-venu.text: Learned at Watts's that it is folly to be on ill terms with those one lives with continually — paid the compositors' fee after weeks of chapel-ghost mischief.

watts-influence-acquired.text: Acquired considerable influence at Watts's — proposed and carried chapel law reforms, led workmen from beer to water-gruel, and was given dispatch work at better pay for speed and reliability.

watts-printing-london.text: Moved from Palmer's to Watts's printing-house near Lincoln's Inn Fields; stayed there for the remainder of the London period.

way-to-wealth-1757.text: In 1757 assembled almanac proverbs into The Way to Wealth — a connected discourse widely copied, reprinted in Britain on broadsides, translated into French twice, and distributed by clergy to the poor.

webb-betrayed-newspaper-plan.text: Webb, told in confidence of Franklin's newspaper plan, immediately revealed it to Keimer, who launched rival proposals — a foolish disclosure Franklin regretted.

whitefield-civil-friendship.text: Maintained a civil, sincere friendship with Whitefield until his death — no religious connection; Whitefield prayed for Franklin's conversion but never believed it answered; Franklin offered his house as lodging, noting it was not for Christ's sake.

whitefield-integrity-trusted.text: Vouches for Whitefield's complete honesty and integrity — never had the least suspicion, despite accusations; testimony the stronger for having no religious connection.

whitefield-orphan-house-disagreement.text: Advised Whitefield to build the Georgia Orphan House in Philadelphia and bring children there, rather than shipping expensive materials to Georgia — the advice was rejected; Franklin therefore refused to contribute initially.

whitefield-writing-hurt-reputation.text: Observed that Whitefield's published writings gave critics a target to diminish his reputation — concludes he would have left a larger, more lasting sect had he never written anything.

writing-arithmetic-school.text: Learned fair writing under Mr. George Brownell but failed in arithmetic.
